p.seg: "Halting Clouds"
Halting clouds -
Longing for dear friends.
Wine vessels brim with fresh brew,
The garden arrays its first blooms,
Wishing to speak but unable to follow through,
Sighs soak my lapel.
Thick, thick the halting clouds,
Drizzling the seasonal rain.
All directions share the gloom.
Level roads are thus blocked.
Quietly I lean on the eastern porch,
Alone I stroke the spring wine.
Good friends are distant and far,
Scratching my head, I stand waiting long.
Halting clouds so dense,
Seasonal rain misty.
All directions share the gloom,
Level land turns to rivers.
Wine I have, wine I have,
Leisurely I drink by the east window.
Wishing to speak of missing someone,
But no boat or carriage follows.
Trees in the eastern garden,
Their branches bloom again.
Competing in fresh beauty,
To delight my feelings.
People also have a saying,
The sun and moon march on.
How can we sit close together,
And talk about our lifelong stories?
Graceful flying birds,
Rest on the trees in my courtyard.
Folding their wings, they pause at leisure,
Their lovely calls harmonize.
Are there no others?
But I think of you truly much.
Wishing to speak but not attained,
How I embrace this regret!
"The Flow of Seasons"
The flow of seasons -
Wandering in late spring.
Spring attire already complete,
Scenery harmonious thus,
Accompanying my shadow alone I roam,
Joy and sighing interweave in my heart.
Far-reaching the flow of seasons,
Solemn the fine morning.
Donning my spring garments,
I head to the eastern outskirts.
Mountains cleansed of lingering haze,
Sky veiled by thin clouds.
A wind comes from the south,
It wings those new sprouts.
Vast, the level ford,
There I rinse and wash.
Distant the far scenery,
Full of delight, full of gaze.
Speaking as my heart desires,
One can also be easily content.
Raising this cup of wine,
Intoxicated with joy, I delight myself.
Gazing toward the midstream,
Long and serene the clear Yí River.
Youths and capped ones finish their studies,
Leisurely chanting, they return.
I love their tranquility,
Awake or asleep, it stirs me.
Only regret we live in different eras,
Far beyond pursuit.
This morning, this evening,
I rest in my cottage.
Flowers and herbs arrayed in rows,
Woods and bamboos lush and dense.
A clear zither lies across the bed,
Unfiltered wine fills half the pot.
The era of Huángdì and Tángyáo is beyond reach,
Sighing alone rests with me.
"The Flourishing Tree"
The flourishing tree -
Thinking of approaching old age.
Sun and moon push forward,
Already it's summer again,
Since childhood I heard of the Way,
With white hair, nothing achieved.
Lush, lush the flourishing tree,
Its roots anchored here.
At dawn it shines with blossoms,
By evening already lost.
Human life is like a sojourn,
Haggardness comes at times.
Quietly speaking, deeply thoughtful,
My heart is full of sorrow.
Lush, lush the flourishing tree,
Here it puts down roots.
Luxuriant blooms rise at dawn,
Sighing, by dusk they're gone.
Steadfastness or fragility lies with humans,
Fortune and misfortune have no fixed gate.
If not the Way, what to rely on?
If not goodness, what to uphold?
Alas, I, a mere youngster,
Endowed with this stubborn simplicity.
Passing years have flowed away,
My achievements haven't grown past the old.
Aspiring to that unceasing pursuit,
How can I be content with daily indulgence?
In my bosom of thoughts,
I'm pained by inner shame.
The ancient teacher's remaining teachings,
How could I let them fall?
At forty, still unknown,
This is nothing to fear!
Grease my famed carriage,
Whip my famed steed,
A thousand miles though remote,
Who dares not to reach!
To the Duke of Chángshā, My Clan Ancestor
"To the Duke of Chángshā, My Clan Ancestor"
The Duke of Chángshā is my clan ancestor,
Both descended from the Grand Marshal.
Generations have grown distant,
We've become like strangers.
Passing through Xúnyáng,
At parting, I present this.
From the same source, streams divide,
People change, generations drift apart.
Sighing with sudden realization,
I recall those very beginnings.
Ritual bonds have faded long,
Years and months have silently passed.
Moved by this journey,
Fondly I hesitate.
O solemn, noble clan,
Truly building this hall.
Harmonious spirit, warm in winter,
Reflecting hearts like jade tablets.
Then plucking spring flowers,
Also heeding autumn frost.
I say with reverence,
Truly the glory of our lineage.
As for my encounter,
In length, I forgot our common root.
Laughter and talk not long,
Soon we part, east and west.
Far, far the Three Xiāngs,
Torrential the Jiǔjiāng River.
Mountains and rivers block the distance,
May messages often get through!
How to express my heart?
I leave these words.
Though adding a basket of earth is slight,
In the end, it builds a mountain.
Reverently, O departing one,
On the road, feel the sorrow.
Our heartfelt talk may be distant,
But let news lead the way!
"In Reply to Dīng of Cháisāng"
A guest, a guest,
Comes and stays.
Upholding integrity, administering wisdom,
Bestowing kindness over a hundred lǐ.
Embracing excellence as returning home,
Hearing goodness as if for the first time.
Not only in harmony,
Often we have fine outings.
Speaking and gazing,
To express my cares.
Once meeting we release joy,
Drunk, then we rest.
Truly delighted at heart's accord,
Just now following me in wander.
"In Reply to Adjutant Páng"
Páng served as adjutant to the garrison army,
On a mission from Jiānglíng to the capital,
Passing through Xúnyáng, he gifted me a poem.
Under the humble gate,
There is a zither, there are books.
I play and I chant,
Thus finding my joy.
Are there no other pleasures?
I delight in this secluded dwelling.
Mornings I tend the garden,
Evenings I recline in my thatched hut.
What people treasure,
May sometimes lack true worth.
Without shared affection,
How can closeness come forth?
I seek a worthy friend,
And truly meet one I hold dear.
Our joyful hearts in deep accord,
As neighbors dwelling near.
Ah, this friend I cherish,
Virtue delights him tirelessly.
I have fine wine prepared,
To share joy with thee.
Then we share fine words,
And compose new poetry.
A single day apart,
Brings longing endlessly.
Our fine outings not yet weary,
Yet vows of parting arise.
I see you off on the road,
Wine cup in hand, no joy in my eyes.
Nostalgic for old Chǔ lands,
Distant western clouds afar.
As you journey far away,
When shall I hear your words, so rare?
When we parted long ago,
Orioles sang their springtime song;
Now we meet again,
Amidst sleet and snow along.
The great fief has its orders,
Sending you to the capital above.
How could I forget feasts and ease?
But royal duties allow no rest thereof.
The cold sun dim and bleak,
The winds solemn and austere.
That boat glides swiftly,
Floating on the river here.
Take care, O traveler,
Think of the end from the start.
Revere these fine hours,
And guard your life with heart.
"Encouraging Farming"
In the distant ancient past,
When humans first were born,
Proud and self-sufficient,
Holding simplicity, true and unadorned.
Once cunning and craft emerged,
Means of sustenance had no base.
Who provided for them?
Truly, it was the wise sage.
Who were these sages?
They, like Hòu Jì in their age;
How did they provide?
By sowing seeds and tilling the ground's stage.
Shùn himself plowed the fields,
Yǔ also farmed with care.
As distant as the Zhōu classics tell,
Among eight policies, food was first to fare.
The cheerful, lovely sounds,
The lush and rolling plains.
Flowers and trees flourish,
Balmy breezes, clear and serene reigns.
Men and women in crowds,
Race with the season, fast and keen.
Mulberry-picking women journey by night,
Farmers lodge in fields, unseen.
Seasons pass too easily,
Mild rains are hard to prolong.
Jì Quē worked with his wife,
Jǔ and Nì coupled strong.
Observe those worthy and wise,
Still toil in fields along.
How much more should common folk,
Avoid idleness, so wrong!
People's lives depend on diligence,
Diligence leaves no want behind.
Feasting in self-indulgence,
What hope at year's end will you find?
Without stored grain, even a dàn's measure,
Hunger and cold will arrive together.
Look upon your fellow men,
Can you not feel shame, whatsoever?
Confucius immersed in virtue's way,
Disdained Fán Xū's farming display;
Dǒng Zhòngshū delighted in lute and books,
Never setting foot in gardens' nooks.
If one can rise above it all,
Following a lofty path's call,
How dare I not straighten my gown,
And revere such virtue's renown?
Naming My Son
"Naming My Son"
Long, long ago, my ancestor,
From Táo Táng's era came.
Distantly, as Yú's guest,
Through generations, brilliance aflame.
Yù Lóng served Xià with zeal,
Shǐ Wéi aided Shāng's reign.
The solemn Sītú,
Made our clan prosper and sustain.
In the chaotic Warring States,
The fading Zhōu, dim and remote.
Phoenixes hid in woods,
Hermits dwelt in hills, remote.
Soaring dragons circled clouds,
Fleeing whales startled the river's note.
Heaven favored the Hàn,
Caring for Mǐn Hóu, our kin.
O glorious Mǐn Hóu,
Destined to aid the rising dragon's win.
Sword in hand, he marched at dawn,
Displaying martial prowess within.
Sworn over mountains and rivers,
He opened lands, his fief to begin.
The diligent Chéngxiàng,
Truly followed the path laid in.
Vast, the long river's source,
Lush, the great tree's bough.
Many streams guided forth,
Countless branches arranged now.
Times have speech and silence,
Fate has rise and fall, anyhow.
In our Jìn dynasty's midst,
Deeds flourished in Chángshā's vow.
Majestic Chángshā,
With merit and virtue endowed.
The emperor rewarded us,
To campaign in the south, allowed.
Success achieved, he resigned,
Unmoved by favor, humble and proud.
Who would think such a heart,
Could be found in recent crowd?
Reverent was my grandfather,
Cautious from start to end.
Upright in both courts,
Benevolent, miles to extend.
O, my benevolent father,
Serene and void, his spirit to send.
Dwelling amidst winds and clouds,
Beyond joy and anger, his transcend.
Alas, I, lacking in grace,
Gaze afar, but cannot ascend.
Ashamed of my graying hair,
Standing alone, with shadow to tend.
Of the three thousand offenses,
Having no heir is most urgent to mend.
Truly, I ponder this,
Hearing your cry, my heart to rend.
Divination foretold a fine day,
The omen also a good hour.
I name you Yǎn,
And style you Qiú Sī, with power.
Be gentle and respectful day and night,
Remember this, every hour.
I recall Kǒng Jí still,
Hoping you'll emulate his power.
Like the child born in night,
Quickly seeking a light;
All who have a heart,
Feel this, not I alone in plight.
Since I've seen you born,
I truly wish you to be right.
As the saying goes,
This feeling needs no proof in sight.
Days and months pass by,
Gradually, you leave childhood behind.
Fortune does not come in vain,
But disaster arrives unkind.
Rise early, retire late,
Hoping you'll be talented and refined;
If you prove not to be so,
Then let it be, resigned!
"Returning Birds"
Fluttering, the returning birds,
Leave the woods at dawn.
Far to the eight horizons,
Near, they rest on cloud-capped lawns.
When gentle winds don't suit,
They turn wings, seeking hearts they've drawn.
Calling to companions, they sing,
Sheltering in clear shades, withdrawn.
Graceful returning birds,
Now soaring, now flying.
Though not longing to wander,
At sight of woods, affection stirs.
Meeting clouds, they rise and dip,
Calling to each other as they return.
Distant roads are truly long,
Yet their nature’s love remains undiminished.
Graceful returning birds
Hover tame around the woods.
Do they think of heavenly paths?
They joy in reaching their old roosts.
Though former mates are gone,
Many voices often harmonize.
In the evening, the air is clear,
And their hearts are carefree.
Graceful returning birds
Fold their wings on cold branches.
They roam not in open woods,
But perch on dense treetops to rest.
Morning breezes stir pure zest,
Lovely calls exchanged at times.
How could snares and arrows harm them?
Having folded wings, why toil?
"Form, Shadow, and Spirit"
Noble and base, wise and foolish,
All bustle about, cherishing life—
This is deeply deluded.
Thus, I thoroughly describe the sorrows of Form and Shadow,
And let Spirit explain nature to resolve them.
May thoughtful gentlemen
Grasp their essence together.
"Leisurely Living on the Double Ninth, with Preface"
In my leisure, I dwell,
Fond of the name "Double Ninth."
Autumn chrysanthemums fill the garden,
Yet I’ve no means to hold wine.
In vain, I take the nine blooms,
Entrusting my thoughts to words.
Life is short, yet worries abound;
People delight in long life.
Sun and moon arrive in their season,
All cherish this festival’s name.
Dew chills, warm breezes cease,
Air clear, celestial signs bright.
Gone swallows leave no shadow,
Coming wild geese bear lingering cries.
Wine can dispel all cares,
Chrysanthemums curb declining years.
But how can a thatched hut scholar
Merely watch time’s passage in vain?
Dusty cups shame the empty vessel,
Cold blossoms bloom alone.
Gathering my robe, I chant in solitude,
Lost in deep emotion.
Dwelling here brings many joys;
Could lingering lead to no achievement?
"Form to Shadow"
Heaven and earth never perish,
Mountains and rivers never change.
Plants follow constant laws,
Withered or flourished by frost and dew.
They say humans are most wise,
Yet alone, we’re not like this!
Just seen alive in the world,
Suddenly gone, never to return.
Who notices one less person?
Do friends and kin still yearn?
Only possessions remain;
Lifting my eyes, grief overwhelms.
I lack arts to ascend transformed,
Surely this end is undoubted.
I hope you heed my words:
When offered wine, do not refuse.
"Shadow’s Reply to Form"
Preserving life cannot be spoken of,
Nurturing it often proves futile.
I truly wish to roam Kūnlún and Huàshān,
But that path is remote and cut off.
Since meeting you,
We’ve never differed in joy or sorrow.
In shade, we seem to part briefly,
In sunlight, we never separate.
This union can’t last forever—
Sadly, we’ll vanish together.
The body gone, fame too ends;
Thinking of it, my passions burn.
Doing good leaves a legacy of love;
Why not strive for it with all your might?
Wine is said to drown sorrows,
But isn’t that far inferior?
"Spirit’s Explanation"
The great potter has no private power;
All principles manifest themselves.
Humans stand among the three powers—
Is it not because of me?
Though I differ from you both,
We’re born attached to one another.
Bound together, sharing good and ill,
How can I not speak to you?
The Three Sovereigns, great sages—
Where are they now?
Péng Zǔ, who lived long years,
Could not stay forever.
Old and young die the same death;
Wise and foolish share one fate.
Drinking daily might bring forgetfulness,
But does it not shorten life?
Doing good is always praised,
Yet who will sing your praises?
Excessive brooding harms our lives;
Better to yield to fate’s flow.
Ride the waves of great change,
Without joy or fear.
When it’s time to end, just end;
No need to worry alone.
Returning to Dwell in Gardens and Fields
Six Poems
One
"Returning to Dwell in Gardens and Fields: Six Poems"
Young, I never fit the common tune,
My nature always loved hills and mountains.
By mistake, I fell into the dusty net,
Gone for thirteen years away.
A tethered bird yearns for its old woods,
A pond fish longs for its former deep.
I’ve cleared wasteland by the southern wilds,
Keeping simplicity, back to gardens and fields.
My plot extends ten acres square,
A thatched hut of eight or nine rooms.
Elms and willows shade the back yard,
Peach and plum trees line the hall front.
Dim, dim, distant village sights,
Lingering, lingering, smoke from the huts.
A dog barks in deep lanes,
A cock crows atop a mulberry tree.
No dust or clutter in my home grounds;
In bare rooms, plenty of leisure.
Long trapped in a cage,
At last I return to nature.
Two
In the wilds, few worldly ties;
Poor lanes, rare carriage tracks.
By day, I close my bramble gate;
In empty rooms, cut off worldly thoughts.
Now and then in village nooks,
Parting grasses, I come and go with others.
When we meet, no random talk—
Only how the mulberry and hemp grow.
Mulberry and hemp daily grow taller,
My fields daily spread wider.
Always I fear frost or hail coming,
To wither them like weeds.
Three
I plant beans beneath the southern hill;
Grass lush, bean sprouts sparse.
At dawn, I rise to clear the weeds,
Shouldering the hoe, home under the moon.
The path is narrow, plants overgrown;
Evening dew soaks my clothes.
Soaked clothes are no great pity,
If only my wishes aren’t betrayed.
Four
Long since I left my outings to hills and marshes,
Roaming free in woods and wilds for fun.
I try taking my nephews and sons along,
Parting brambles, pacing through ruined sites.
Wandering among the mounds and ridges,
Lingering traces of former dwellings.
Wells and stoves left in spots,
Mulberry, bamboo—rotting stumps remain.
I ask a wood-gatherer,
"Where have all these people gone?"
The wood-gatherer tells me,
"Dead and gone, none are left."
"A generation changes court and market"—
These words are truly not false.
Human life is like illusion,
In the end, it returns to nothingness.
Five
Disconsolate, I return alone, my staff in hand,
Through rugged paths, past overgrown bushes I've spanned.
The mountain stream runs clear and shallow,
Where I can wash my feet and wallow.
I strain my newly brewed wine with care,
And with a single chicken, neighbors I ensnare.
As the sun sets, the room turns dim,
Thorny firewood replaces the candle's brim.
Joy comes, yet the night seems too brief to implore,
Before I know it, dawn is at the door.
Six
I sow seedlings east by the riverbank,
They sprout and fill the paths, rank by rank.
Though weary from hoeing, I bear the strain,
With coarse wine, I ease my pain.
At dusk, I board my firewood-laden cart,
The road grows dark, as daylight does depart.
Returning, I gaze at the distant smoke's art,
My young child waits by the eaves, playing his part.
You ask what drives me to this life so plain,
A hundred years of toil, not in vain.
I only hope the hemp and mulberry thrive,
In silkworm month, to spin and weave alive.
Such is my simple heart's true plea,
To open paths for friends who'll join me.
Asking the Messenger
"Asking the Messenger"
You come from the mountains, so they say,
At dawn or dusk, from Tiānmù on your way.
Beneath my southern window, in gentle array,
How many clusters of chrysanthemums bloom today?
The rose leaves have already begun to spread,
Autumn orchids' fragrance is widely shed.
Return to the mountains, where I long to be led,
There, the wine should be ripe, as it's often said.
"Roaming Xié Chuān"
On the fifth day of the first month, Xīnyǒu year,
The weather clear and serene, without a fear,
The scenery tranquil and beautiful, ever so dear.
With two or three neighbors, I hold near,
Together we roam Xié Chuān, far and near.
By the long flowing stream, we stand in cheer,
Gazing at Céngchéng, its presence sincere.
Bream and carp leap with scales aglow as dusk draws here,
Water gulls ride the gentle breeze, soaring without a peer.
That southern mound, old in name and fact,
No longer merits sighs, that's the pact.
But as for Céngchéng, alone it's stacked,
With no reliance, purely intact,
It stands splendid mid the plain, a solitary act.
I recall the divine mountains, a distant impact,
Admiring its fine name, my heart's attract.
Joyful yet insufficient, that's the fact,
I casually compose a poem, on impulse I act.
Lamenting how days and months have passed by,
Mourning that my years won't stay, they fly.
Each records their age and homeland with a sigh,
To mark this moment, as time goes high.
The new year suddenly brings fifty to my door,
My life approaches its end, forevermore.
Thinking of this stirs my heart to the core,
So I seize the day for this tour.
The air is mild, the sky purely clear,
We sit in rows by the distant river, near.
Gentle rapids speed the patterned bream,
Quiet valleys lift the crying gulls' dream.
Over wide marshes, my wandering eyes gleam,
Gazing distantly at Céng Hill, it seems.
Though not as grand as the nine-layered peak,
Looking around, no match do I seek.
I lift the pot to greet friends, mild and meek,
Fill the cups, toast after toast, we speak.
Who knows from now on, if ever again,
Such moments we'll attain?
Mid-cup, I let distant feelings reign,
Forgetting the worries of a thousand years' chain.
Let's indulge in today's joy, not in vain,
Tomorrow's cares, I won't entertain.
To Zhōu Xùzhī, Zǔ Qǐ, and Xiè Jǐngyí, the Three Gentlemen
While the three were lecturing on rites and collating texts
"To Zhōu Xùzhī, Zǔ Qǐ, and Xiè Jǐngyí, the Three Gentlemen, While They Were Lecturing on Rites and Collating Texts"
Laden with illness, under the sagging eaves I lie,
All day long, not a single joy comes by.
When medicines give occasional rest,
I think of those in my heart, the best.
We're not far apart in ordinary measure,
Yet the road is distant, for what reason?
Zhōu expounds the teachings of Confucius with pleasure,
Zǔ and Xiè respond, coming together.
The Way has been lost for nearly a thousand years,
Today, I hear it again, calming fears.
The stable yard is no place for lectures clear,
Yet collating texts, you've been sincere.
As an old man, I have affections dear,
Wishing to be your neighbor, ever near;
I hope to impart words to you all,
Follow me by the Yǐng River's call.
"Begging for Food"
Hunger drives me out the door,
Not knowing where to go, or what for!
Walking on, I reach this village's core,
Knocking on doors, my words clumsy and poor.
The host understands my plight,
His gift isn't in vain, shining bright.
We talk from day till night,
Whenever wine comes, I drink with delight.
Joyful in this new friendship's light,
I chant and compose poems with all my might.
Moved by your kindness, like the washerwoman's deed,
Ashamed I lack Hán's talent in my need.
How to thank you, my gratitude I embed,
In the afterlife, I'll repay, as it's said.
"Strolling with Friends Under the Cypress Trees at the Zhōu Family Graves"
The weather's fine today, so clear,
With pure music and strings we hear.
Moved by those beneath the cypress shade,
How can we not be merry, unafraid?
Fresh songs scatter new melodies around,
Green wine brings smiles, joy is found.
Unknown what tomorrow may hold,
But for now, my heart is content and bold.
"Poem of Lament in Chǔ Mode, Shown to Attendant Clerk Páng and Administrator Dèng"
The ways of Heaven are dark and remote,
Ghosts and spirits, obscure and anecdote.
Since youth, I've strived for good deeds,
Toiling hard for fifty-four years, it leads.
At twenty, I met worldly strife,
In my thirties, I lost my wife.
Fiery blazes often raged and spread,
Pests ran rampant in the fields I tread.
Storms and rains came crashing down,
Harvests didn't fill a single town.
Summer days, I long endure hunger's pain,
Cold nights, without a blanket, I remain.
At dusk, I yearn for the cock's crow,
At dawn, I wish the sun would slow.
In myself, why blame Heaven's will?
Yet sorrows before me, bitter and chill.
Alas, for fame after I'm gone,
To me, it's like fleeting smoke at dawn.
Passionately, I sing a sad song alone,
Believing Zhōng Zǐqī would understand, as shown.
"In Reply to Cānjūn Páng"
Thrice I've read your gift, with thoughtful mind,
Unable to stop, though I'm inclined.
Since we became neighbors, you and I,
Winter and spring have passed by.
Our sincere talks, so genuine and true,
Suddenly made old friends of us two.
As the saying goes among the crowd,
A few meetings make kinship allowed.
How much more when feelings soar so high?
Human affairs often go awry,
And now we must say goodbye.
What Lord Yáng sighed about in his day,
Isn't just ordinary grief, I'd say.
I've been ill for many a year,
No longer writing, far and near.
My foundation was never rich or vast,
And now old age and sickness hold me fast.
Following the rite of mutual exchange in Zhōu's past,
I write this for missing thoughts that will last.
Friendship need not be old to be profound,
A moment's meeting can common ground.
You appreciate my tastes, I've found,
Often visiting my garden round.
Our talks are free from vulgar sound,
Discoursing on sages' texts renowned.
Sometimes with several dou of wine,
We drink at leisure, feeling fine.
I am a recluse, truly so,
No more east-west ties to undergo.
Things may be new, but friends are old,
The weak brush has much to unfold.
Hearts connect beyond miles untold,
Though bodies are by rivers and mountains controlled.
Take care of your health, precious and bold,
When shall we meet again, as of old?
"Composed on the First Day of the Fifth Month, in Response to Registrar Dài"
The empty boat drifts with carefree oars,
Turning back, it seems without end.
The year begins with a glance up and down,
The cycle of stars is nearly at its midpoint.
Rare withered things by the southern window,
The northern woods flourish and abound.
The divine spring pours seasonal rain,
Morning hues play the soothing wind.
What comes must eventually go,
Such is the inevitable way of human life.
Living ordinarily, awaiting its end,
Bending an arm as a pillow—does it harm simplicity?
Change may bring ease or hardship,
Yet following one's will, no high or low matters.
In such a state, one is already elevated,
Why must one climb Huà or Sōng peaks?
Drinking Alone During Continuous Rain
"Drinking Alone During Continuous Rain"
Destined life meets its end,
This has been said since ancient times.
In the world, there are immortals like Sōng and Qiáo,
Where are they now, I wonder?
An elder friend gifted me wine,
Saying drinking could make one an immortal;
A sip distances all worldly worries,
Another cup, and heaven is forgotten.
But how could heaven be far away?
Embracing truth, nothing takes precedence.
Cloud-riding cranes have wondrous wings,
They traverse the eight directions in a moment.
Holding fast to this solitude,
I've toiled diligently for forty years.
My body has long transformed,
What more can words say, with my heart still here?
First
"Two Poems on Moving House"
Long I wished to dwell in Náncūn,
Not for divining the abode's fortune.
Hearing many sincere-hearted people lived there,
I delighted to share mornings and evenings with them.
Harboring this wish for years,
Today I finally undertake the move.
Why must a humble home be spacious?
Enough to shelter bed and mat.
Neighbors often come by,
Engaging in candid talks of the past.
Marvelous writings we admire together,
Puzzling meanings we analyze as one.
Second
Spring and autumn abound with fine days,
I climb high and compose new poems.
Passing gates, we call out to each other,
When there's wine, we pour and share it.
After farm work, each returns home,
In leisure, we miss one another;
Missing, then we don our robes,
Chatting and laughing, never tiring.
Such joy is beyond compare,
Do not lightly leave this behind.
Food and clothing must be managed,
Toiling the fields will not deceive me.
"In Response to Liú Cháisāng"
Long have the hills and marshes called me,
Why then do I hesitate?
Simply for the sake of kin and old friends,
I cannot bear to speak of living alone.
Fine days stir wondrous thoughts,
Staff in hand, I return to my western hut.
Deserted paths see no returning souls,
Ruins appear here and there.
Thatched roof repaired and settled,
New fields await their tilling.
Valley winds turn bleak and biting,
Spring wine eases hunger and toil.
A frail daughter, though not a son,
Comforts the heart—better than none.
Restless affairs of the world,
Years and months drift apart with them.
Farming and weaving suffice for needs,
What more beyond this is required?
Onward, a hundred years hence,
Body and name alike will vanish.
"In Reply to Liú Cháisāng"
In seclusion, few visits I receive,
Often forgetting the seasons' full cycle.
The courtyard strewn with fallen leaves,
Sighing, I know autumn has come.
Fresh sunflowers thrive by the north wall,
Fine grains ripple in southern fields.
If I seek no joy now,
Who knows if next year will arrive?
Bid my wife bring the young ones,
On a fine day, we'll journey afar.
First
"Two Poems in Response to Guō Zhǔbù"
Lush woods before the hall,
Midsummer stores cool shade within.
Gentle winds arrive in season,
Whirlwinds open wide my robe.
Ceasing social ties, I roam in leisurely pursuits,
Rising or resting, I play with books and lute.
Garden vegetables grow in abundance,
Last year's grain still stored today.
Providing for oneself has its limits,
Excess is not what I admire.
Pounding glutinous rice for fine wine,
When it's ready, I pour my own cup.
My young child plays by my side,
Babbling words not yet formed.
Such things truly bring joy,
Enough to forget ornate hairpins.
Gazing afar at the white clouds,
How deep my thoughts of antiquity.
Second
Gentle rains graced the three springs,
Now pure and cool, the autumn season.
Dew condenses, no wandering mists,
Sky high, scenery clear and bright.
Hills and peaks tower with graceful summits,
Viewed from afar, all wondrous and steep.
Fragrant chrysanthemums bloom, lighting the woods,
Green pines crown the cliffs in rows.
Cherishing this chaste and splendid grace,
Eminent, heroes under frost.
Holding my cup, I think of recluses,
For a thousand years, I've upheld your way.
Examining my plain life, no achievements gained,
Listless, I pass this fine month.
"Farewell to a Guest at Wáng Fǔjūn's Banquet"
Autumn days, bleak and harsh,
All flowers have withered away.
Thus, in the season of frost underfoot,
I climb high to bid farewell.
Chill air envelops hills and marshes,
Wandering clouds suddenly rootless.
Isles and shores stretch far and wide,
Wind and water part in discord.
Gazing at dusk, longing for a fine feast,
Parting words only deepen sorrow.
Morning birds return by evening,
The setting sun gathers its last rays.
Going and staying—paths diverge,
Turning my carriage, I linger in regret.
Eyes follow the receding boat afar,
Heart drifts with all transformations.
"Farewell to Yīn Jìn'ān"
Yīn first served as Adjutant to the Chief Clerk of Jìn'ān's Southern Prefecture,
Thus residing in Xúnyáng.
Later, he became Adjutant to the Grand Commandant,
Moving his family eastward,
I write this to present to him.
Friendships may not last long,
Yet one meeting fills us with warmth.
Staying over, we shared pure conversations,
Growing ever closer in kinship.
Last year, my home was in Nánlǐ,
Briefly we were neighbors for a time.
Leaning on my staff, I roamed with you freely,
Lingering, forgetting night and dawn.
Speech and silence differ by circumstance,
I knew we'd have to part.
Not thinking it would come so soon,
The thought arises this spring.
Fluttering, the west wind arrives,
Drifting, eastern clouds depart.
Mounts and rivers span a thousand miles,
Laughter and talk hard to sustain.
A fine talent won't hide from the world,
While rivers and lakes harbor the lowly and poor.
Should you have chance to pass by,
Remember to visit an old friend.
"To Senior Clerk Yáng"
Senior Clerk Yáng of the Left Army,
On a mission to Qínchuān,
I write this for him.
Born after three dynasties' decline,
I long for Huángdì and Yú's reign with a sigh.
To learn of millennia beyond my time,
I rely on ancient books held high.
Sages left traces of their days,
In the central capital, in myriad ways.
How could I forget to roam with heart and sight?
But rivers and passes block my flight.
Now the nine realms are unified,
I'll ready my boat and cart to ride.
Hearing you'll set forth before long,
Illness keeps me from going along.
If your route passes Shāngshān's way,
For me, pause and linger, I pray.
Offer my thanks to Qǐ and Jiǎo, I implore,
How fares their spirited essence as of yore?
Who now picks purple mushrooms rare,
Deep valleys long deserted and bare?
Four horses bring no guarantee from strife,
Poverty and lowliness can entertain life.
Pure songs bond deeply in my heart,
But men part, and fate plays its part.
Holding feelings through generations passed,
Words end, but thoughts forever last.
"Year's End, in Harmony with Attendant Zhāng"
The court mourns men of old, a somber scene,
Swift steeds grieve at the fountain of sorrow, keen.
Tomorrow differs from today's light,
At year's end, what can I say in my plight?
Pale face loses its radiant sheen,
White hair has flourished, thick and clean.
How naive was Duke Mù of Qín's claim,
Could physical strength remain the same?
Towards evening, a strong wind does rise,
Cold clouds veil the western skies.
The air turns sharp, biting and severe,
Birds fly back, in disarray and fear.
Human life is seldom long and stable,
Especially when woes make it unbearable.
Often lacking clear wine to partake,
Nothing to cheer the present, for old times' sake.
Wealth or poverty, no constant care,
Haggardness comes with change, hard to bear.
Reflecting on myself, deep feelings swell,
Facing fate, my sighs and sorrows compel.
"In Response to Hú Xīcáo, Shown to Cáo Cáo the Bandit"
In the fifth month, when Ruíbīn prevails,
A clear dawn brings southern gentle gales.
Not too fast, nor too slow they blow,
Fluttering lightly, making my clothes flow.
Layers of clouds obscure the bright sun,
Leisurely rain falls, a subtle one.
My gaze wanders to the western garden's space,
Where purple mallows bloom with vibrant grace.
Now they are lovely, beyond compare,
But alas, they'll wither, fade, and despair.
Moved by things, I wish to seize the hour,
But regret having no means to empower.
Longingly waiting for autumn's yield,
Desolate, delayed, in barren field.
Wild thoughts I cannot hold at bay,
In reckless sorrow, I mourn and stray.
Lament for My Cousin Zhòngdé
"Lament for My Cousin Zhòngdé"
Bearing grief, I pass the old abode,
Sad tears fall as my heart's heavy load.
Ask for whom this sorrow I bear?
For one in the netherworld, beyond compare.
In kinship rites, among the clan he stood,
Our affection deep, as if of same blood.
When we held hands before the gate,
Who'd have thought you'd meet such a fate?
In the count of life, none can evade,
Like a mountain unfinished, efforts fade.
A grieving mother sinks in pain,
Two young heirs, but toddlers they remain.
Two plaques left in the empty hall,
Morning and night, no weeping call.
Dust gathers on vacant seats, untold,
Wild grasses overrun the courtyard old.
Steps and paths lack footprints of play,
In the garden, my lone feelings stay.
Fading away with nature's course,
Never to return in bodily force.
Slowly, I turn to take my leave,
Sorrow fills my heart, making me grieve.
"First Appointment as Army Adviser, Passing Qū'ē"
In youth, I dwelt apart from worldly affairs,
My heart entrusted to zithers and books, no cares.
Clad in coarse cloth, content and free,
Often empty-handed, yet calm as can be.
When chance arose, as if by fate's design,
I lingered sweetly on the thoroughfare's line.
Laying aside my staff, I packed at dawn,
Briefly leaving garden and field, forlorn.
A lone boat drifts into the distance, slight,
Endless thoughts of return, winding and tight.
My journey is not short, by any measure,
Climbing over a thousand li, no leisure.
Eyes weary of strange rivers and trails,
My heart yearns for mountain and marsh hails.
Gazing at clouds, I shame the high-flying bird,
By the water, I envy the swimming herd.
True thoughts were always in my heart,
Who says physical bounds can keep us apart?
For now, I'll follow nature's changing way,
And return to Bān's hut at close of day.
One
"Two Poems on Returning from the Capital in the Fifth Month of the Gēngzǐ Year, Detained by Wind at Guīlín"
On and on, I follow the homeward track,
Counting days, longing for the old house back.
First joy, to serve my mother's gentle face,
Then delight, to see my brothers in their place.
Rowing through winding paths, we go,
The sun limits the western sky's glow.
Rivers and mountains, perilous indeed,
A returning son minds the path ahead with heed.
The south wind betrays my heart's desire,
Moored oars, by the desolate lake, I tire.
Tall grasses stretch with no end in sight,
Summer trees stand alone, dense and bright.
Who says the traveler's boat is far away?
Gazing near, a hundred li holds sway.
Straining my eyes, I recognize the southern ridge,
In vain I sigh, whereto does my path bridge?
Two
Since ancient times, travel tolls are sighed,
Only now do I feel it deep inside.
How vast the mountains and rivers appear,
Winds and waters, hard to predict, I fear.
Crashing waves roar, reaching the sky,
Endless winds, without a lull, pass by.
Long away, I miss where I was born,
Why am I stranded here, forlorn?
Quietly thinking, gardens and woods are best,
The mortal world, truly, I can detest.
How many years does one's prime allow?
Follow your heart, why hesitate now?
Returning to Jiānglíng in the Seventh Month of the Xīnchǒu Year, Traveling at Night to Túkǒu
"Returning to Jiānglíng in the Seventh Month of the Xīnchǒu Year, Traveling at Night to Túkǒu"
Thirty years of leisurely stay,
Far from worldly dust, in disarray.
Poetry and books deepened old delights,
Groves and gardens, free of vulgar plights.
Why leave this behind, I implore,
To distant Southern Jīng, I must explore!
Rapping the oar under the new autumn moon,
By the stream, I bid friends farewell soon.
Cool winds rise as dusk draws near,
Night scenes clear and bright appear:
Vast and bright, the sky's expanse,
Glistening and calm, the river's dance.
Burdened by duties, no time for sleep,
At midnight, alone, my journey I keep.
Singing for office is not my part,
Attached to farming, with all my heart.
Discard my cap, return to the old land,
Not by fine titles to be command.
Nurture truth in a humble abode,
Hoping to make a good name bestowed.
One
"Two Poems on Longing for the Ancients at the Farmstead in the Start of Spring of the Guǐmǎo Year"
In past times, I heard of southern fields,
But in those years, never did I tread.
Since some have often been in need,
How can I avoid spring's call, ahead?
At dawn, I prepared my carriage and steed,
Starting the journey, my feelings freed.
Birds chirp, joyous in the new season's air,
Cool breezes send goodness beyond compare.
Cold grasses cover the desolate trail,
The land remote, where few prevail.
Thus, the old man leaning on his staff,
Drifted away, with a tranquil laugh.
In reason, I shame the worldly wise,
What I preserve, how shallow in their eyes?
Two
My late teacher left a teaching:
Worry about the Way, not about poverty.
Looking up, it seems distant and hard to reach,
So I turn to aspire to constant diligence.
Holding the plow, I delight in seasonal tasks,
Smiling, I encourage the farmers.
Level fields meet the distant wind,
Fine sprouts also cherish freshness.
Though I haven't measured the year's harvest,
In these activities, there's much joy.
Farming has its times of rest,
No travelers stop to ask the way.
At sunset, we return together,
Offering wine to reward nearby neighbors.
Chanting long, I close my wooden gate,
Content to be a man of the fields.
Written in the Twelfth Month of the Guǐmǎo Year for My Cousin Jìng Yuǎn
"Written in the Twelfth Month of the Guǐmǎo Year for My Cousin Jìng Yuǎn"
I hide my traces beneath a humble gate,
Far removed from the world's affairs.
Looking around, none know me,
The thornwood door stays closed by day.
Chilly is the year-end wind,
Gloomy, the all-day snow.
Listening closely, it makes no sound,
In sight, it's already pure white.
Bitter cold invades my sleeves,
Simple fare is rarely set.
In this desolate, empty space,
Nothing brings the slightest pleasure.
Reading through books of a thousand years,
Often I see the noble remnants.
Lofty virtues I cannot climb,
But deeply grasp the steadfastness in hardship.
If the broad path is not to be taken,
Is dwelling in obscurity then foolish?
My meaning lies beyond words,
Who can discern this bond?
"Traveling through Qiánxī as Jiànwēi Army Advisor in the Third Month of the Yǐsì Year"
I haven't trod this ground,
Many years have passed.
Morning and evening, I gaze on mountains and rivers,
Everything is just as before.
A light rain washes the tall woods,
A fresh breeze lifts cloud-wings.
Contemplating how all things endure,
The righteous wind remains unseparated.
What am I, after all,
Striving in this duty?
My form seems constrained,
But my true heart cannot be changed.
Daily I dream of garden and field,
How can I long stay parted?
Always yearning for the returning boat,
Truly, I should be like the frost-resistant cypress.
"Returning to My Old Dwelling"
Formerly, I lived in Shàngjīng,
For six years, leaving and returning.
Today I come back again,
Filled with sorrow and grief.
The paths remain unchanged,
But some houses are no more.
Walking through my old home,
Few elderly neighbors remain.
Step by step, I seek past traces,
Some places especially linger in memory.
Flowing illusions in a hundred years,
Cold and heat daily push each other.
Often I fear life's end,
Before my strength has even faded.
Set it aside, think no more,
A cup of wine can briefly dispel cares.
"Encountering Fire in the Sixth Month of the Wùshēn Year"
My thatched hut in a poor lane,
Gladly I left grand carriages.
Midsummer, a swift gale arose,
Instantly, woods and home burned.
Not one room left standing,
A boat shades the front door.
Far into the new autumn night,
The moon stands full and round.
Fruits and vegetables begin to regrow,
Startled birds have not yet returned.
At midnight, I stand in distant thought,
My gaze sweeps the nine heavens.
Since youth, I've held to solitude,
Suddenly over forty years have passed.
My form follows nature's course,
But my spirit remains ever serene.
Integrity is my innate quality,
Jade and stone seem less firm.
I recall the time of Dōnghù,
When surplus grain stayed in the fields.
Full-bellied, with no worries,
They rose at dawn and slept at dusk.
Since I cannot meet that age,
I'll tend my western garden.
"The Ninth Day of the Ninth Month of the Jǐyǒu Year"
Slowly, autumn draws to its close,
Chill winds and dew interweave.
Creeping grasses bloom no more,
Garden trees wither in vain.
Clear air purges lingering haze,
Vast and high, the celestial realm.
Mournful cicadas, no returning sound,
Flocks of wild geese cry beneath the clouds.
All transformations follow one another,
Is human life not toil?
Since ancient times, all meet their end,
Thinking of it, my heart burns.
How to express my feelings?
With turbid wine, I console myself.
A thousand years hence, I cannot know,
Let me prolong this present day.
"Harvesting Early Rice in the Western Field in the Ninth Month of the Gēngxū Year"
Human life returns to constant principles,
Food and clothing are its foundation.
Who can neglect these basics,
And yet seek peace for himself?
At spring's start, I attend to constant work,
The year's yield may then be seen.
At dawn, I go out to light labor,
At sunset, I return with plow on shoulder.
Mountains abound with frost and dew,
The air turns cold early.
Are farming families not suffering?
Yet we cannot escape this hardship.
My limbs are truly weary,
But may no disasters befall.
Washing, I rest beneath the eaves,
A cup of wine eases my heart.
Far removed, the hearts of Jǔ and Nì,
After a thousand years, still connect with mine.
I only wish it could always be so,
Tilling the soil is no regret.
"Harvesting at the Lower Xùn Field Hut in the Eighth Month of the Bǐngchén Year"
In poverty, I rely on farming,
Laboring hard in the eastern forest bend.
I don't speak of spring toil's bitterness,
But often fear failing my aspirations.
The field officer hopes for autumn harvest,
Sending word in harmony with me.
The hungry rejoice at first fullness,
I dress and wait for the cock's crow.
Raising the oar, I cross the calm lake,
Floating along clear streams' curves.
Lush and dense in the wild mountains,
Monkey calls, leisurely and sad.
The mournful wind loves the quiet night,
Forest birds delight at dawn's break.
Since I began this life,
Three or four decades have passed.
My youthful grace has aged,
But my purpose remains unchanged.
From afar, I thank the old man with hoe,
May I join you in dwelling.
Drinking Wine
Twenty Poems
"Drinking Wine"
I live in leisure with little joy,
And lately the nights have grown long,
By chance, I have some fine wine,
And not an evening passes without drinking.
Gazing at my shadow, I drink alone,
Suddenly, I'm drunk again.
After becoming drunk,
I often write a few lines for amusement,
Thus papers and ink have multiplied,
The verses lack order,
I asked an old friend to write them down,
Just for laughter, that's all.
First
Decline and glory have no fixed abode,
They alternate between one another.
Shào Píng in the melon field,
Was he like his time in Dōnglíng?
Cold and heat succeed each other,
Human life is always thus.
The enlightened understand its meaning,
Resolved, they harbor no doubts.
Suddenly, with a cup of wine,
Day and night, I joyfully hold it.
Second
They say accumulation of good deeds brings reward;
Bó Yí and Shū Qí starved on Shǒuyáng's height.
If virtue and vice lack due recompense,
What avails it to preach with all our might?
At ninety, cord-belted, poor, helpless, alone,
How bitter the hunger and cold in his days!
Had he not held fast to his honor, though poor,
His name would have perished long since with its praise.
III
For centuries the Way has been destroyed;
Each man keeps cautious guard over his gain.
They have wine before them but will not drink;
They only fear their reputation's stain.
What makes our life on earth so precious, then?
Is it not that we live but once and die?
How long does our life last us after all?
Swift as a flashing glance it passes by.
In this great turmoil of a hundred years,
What can we hope to achieve in the end?
IV
Restlessly the stray bird
Flies alone at dusk still.
Hovering, uncertain where to rest,
Night after night its cry grows more shrill.
Its piercing call longing for the far distance;
Going and coming, it seems so forlorn.
Now it chances upon a lone pine
And folds its wings, from afar returning.
In the strong wind no lush foliage thrives,
But this pine's shade alone does not decay.
Having found a refuge to settle,
For a thousand years it will not stray.
V
I built my hut within where others dwell,
And yet there is no noise of carts and horses.
You ask me how that can be;
With a mind remote, the region too grows distant.
I pick chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge,
And far away gaze upon the southern mountains.
The mountain air is lovely as the sun sets,
And flocks of flying birds return together.
In these things there is a fundamental truth;
I would explain but have forgotten the words.
VI
Human conduct varies in countless ways;
Who can distinguish the wrong from the right?
Right and wrong, once contrasted,
Echo like thunder, praise and blame alike!
In the Three Dynasties such things were common;
The enlightened man seems not to be so.
Shocking indeed are the vulgar evils;
Better follow Huáng and Qǐ, and go.
VII
The autumn chrysanthemums have lovely hues;
I pluck the petals dripping with dew.
I float them in this care-dispelling stuff
To distance my feelings from the world's turmoil.
Though I drink alone, a single cup,
When the cup is drained, the pot pours itself.
As the sun sets, all movements cease;
Homeward birds hasten to the woods, chirping.
I proudly sing by the eastern eaves;
In this I find my life's meaning again.
VIII
The green pine in the eastern garden
Is hidden by a profusion of grasses.
When harsh frost kills all other plants,
Then its lofty boughs stand out alone.
Amid a connected forest, none notices;
A single tree, and the crowd marvels.
I hang my wine pot on the cold branch,
And from time to time gaze afar.
My life is but a dreamlike illusion;
Why should I be tied by worldly bonds?
IX
At early dawn I heard a knocking at my gate;
In haste I threw on my clothes and opened the door myself.
"Who is it, may I ask, who comes?"
An old farmer with kind intentions.
He brought a jug of wine from afar to see me,
Suspecting that I am out of step with the times.
"In tattered clothes under a thatched roof,
This is no fit place for a lofty dweller.
The whole age is alike in its ways;
I wish you would muddy yourself in their mud."
I am deeply moved by the old man's words,
But my nature is little suited to such harmony.
To rein in one's horse can indeed be learned,
But to go against oneself—is that not delusion?
Let us just enjoy this drinking together;
My carriage cannot be turned back.
X
In the past I once traveled far away,
Until I reached the shores of the Eastern Sea.
The road was long and winding,
Winds and waves blocked my path midway.
What drove me to this journey?
It seemed to be the pangs of hunger.
I strained my body to secure a full meal,
A little sufficed, and I had some to spare.
Fearing this was no plan for reputation,
I halted my carriage and returned to a life of leisure.
XI
Yán Huí was praised as benevolent,
Róng Qǐ was said to possess the Way.
Though often in want, they did not live long,
Suffering hunger till old age.
Though their names remain after death,
Their whole lives were spent in hardship.
After death, what do they know?
To follow one's heart is truly good.
Some nurture their precious bodies,
But at death, their treasures vanish.
Why dislike naked burial?
One should understand the meaning behind it.
XII
Zhǎnggōng once held office,
But his strong principles soon lost their time.
He closed his door and never went out again,
Cutting ties with the world for life.
Zhònglǐ returned to the great marshes,
His lofty style began there.
Once gone, it should be final;
Why hesitate again?
Go, go, what more is there to say?
The world has long been deceptive.
Cast off these endless discussions;
Please follow where I go.
XIII
There was a guest who often stayed with me,
But our choices and rejections were worlds apart.
One man was always drunk,
The other sober all year round.
Sober and drunk still laughed at each other,
Their words neither understanding the other.
How foolish, this cautious conformity!
Aloof and proud seems somewhat wiser.
I say to the one who drinks deeply:
As the sun sets, the candle should blaze.
XIV
An old friend appreciated my tastes,
And brought a jug along to visit.
We spread robes and sat beneath the pine,
After several cups, we were drunk again.
The old men chattered disorderly,
Cups and ladles lost all order.
Unaware of my own existence,
How could I know the value of things?
Lost in the lingering haze of wine,
Therein lies a profound flavor!
XV
Living in poverty, I lack helpers,
Bushes and trees overgrow my dwelling.
Flocks of birds fly about,
But in stillness, no human traces.
How vast and endless the universe!
Human life seldom reaches a hundred.
The years and months press upon us,
My temples have long been white.
If I do not resign myself to poverty or success,
My simple aspirations would be deeply regrettable.
XVI
In youth, I had little to do with worldly affairs,
My delight was in the Six Classics.
As I approached forty,
I lingered and achieved nothing.
I held fast to the principle of enduring poverty,
Experiencing hunger and cold to the full.
My humble hut is swept by mournful winds,
Wild grasses cover the front courtyard.
Clad in coarse cloth, I guard the long night,
But the morning cock refuses to crow.
Mèng Gōng is not here now,
So my feelings remain obscured forever.
XVII
The secluded orchid grows in the front courtyard,
Waiting for the clear breeze to release its fragrance.
When the clear breeze suddenly arrives,
It stands out from the common weeds.
Progressing, I lose the old path;
Following the Way, perhaps I can get through.
Awakened, I should think of returning,
Before the birds are gone and the good bow is discarded.
XVIII
Zǐ Yún had a nature addicted to wine,
But his home was poor and he had no means to obtain it.
Occasionally, he relied on well-meaning people,
Who brought ale to dispel his perplexities.
When the cup came, he would drain it dry,
And every inquiry he would fully satisfy;
At times, unwilling to speak,
Was it not about waging war against states?
A benevolent man uses his heart,
Never failing in expression or silence.
Nineteen
In the past, I suffered from constant hunger,
Left my plow to pursue an official career.
Unable to maintain moderation in sustenance,
Cold and hunger persistently plagued me.
At that time, approaching thirty,
My aspirations were filled with shame.
Thus, I firmly resolved,
To return to the fields until death.
Slowly, the stars and seasons flow,
Quietly, another twelve years have passed.
The world's path is vast and endless,
Which is why Yáng Zhū stopped.
Though I lack the means to scatter gold,
I can still rely on coarse wine.
Twenty

Throughout the world, few remain true!
The diligent old man of Lǔ,
Mended the age to restore its purity.
Though the phoenix did not come,
Rites and music were briefly renewed.
The faint echoes ceased at Zhū Sì,
Drifting until the mad Qín dynasty.
What crime did the Books of Songs and Documents commit,

Those earnest old scholars,
Worked diligently at their task.
How, in this forsaken age,

All day, carriages rush about,

"Stopping Wine"
Dwelling near the city walls,
Leisurely and at ease I rest.
Sitting rest under high shade,
Walking rest within my humble gate.
Good flavors rest with garden mallows,
Greatest joys rest with young children.
All my life, I have not stopped wine,
Stopping wine brings no joy.
Stopping at night, I cannot sleep peacefully,
Stopping at dawn, I cannot rise.
Every day I wish to stop it,
But my vitality stops functioning.
Only know that stopping is unhappy,
Not knowing that stopping benefits oneself.
Now I begin to see stopping as good,
This very day, I truly stop.
From now on, I stop and go,
Will stop by the Fú Sāng's shore.
My clear face stops its usual expression,
How can it last a thousand ages?

"Narrating Wine"
Double Li shines on the southern land,
The calls of phoenixes are heard.
Though autumn grass has not yet yellowed,
The warm wind has long parted.
White pebbles gleam on long sandbars,
On Nán Yuè, no clouds remain;
Yù Zhāng rises against high gates,
Chóng Huá rests in his spiritual tomb.
Shedding tears, I sigh within,
Listening intently for the dawn.
Divine land offers fine grain,
The western spirit is tamed for me.
Zhū Liáng commanded the army,
Mi Shěng lost his life.
Shān Yáng returned to a lesser state,
Yet his fame was hardly earned.
Diviner Shēng tended this pasture well,
Content, he did not act as ruler.
Píng Wáng left the old capital,
In the gorge, he embraced the lingering fragrance.
Twin suns just began to nurture,
Three-legged bird revealed strange writings.
Prince Jīng loved pure melodies,
At midday, he soared over Hé Fén.
Lord Zhū practiced the ninefold breath,
In idle retirement, free from worldly chaos.
Towering within the western ridges,
He rests often with his dear ones.
Heaven's countenance endures forever,
Péng Zǔ's longevity and early death are not equal.
Blaming My Sons
Shū Yǎn, Xuān Sì, Yōng Fèn, Duān Yì, Tōng Tōng,
Five in all,
Shū, Xuān, Yōng, Duān, Tōng,
Are all their childhood names.
"Blaming My Sons"
White hair covers my temples,
My skin no longer firm.
Though I have five sons,
None care for books and brush.
Ā Shū is already sixteen,
His laziness unmatched.
Ā Xuān approaches fifteen,
Yet shows no love for arts.
Yōng and Duān, both thirteen,
Cannot tell six from seven.
Tōng Zǐ, nearly nine,
Only seeks pears and chestnuts.
If heaven's will is thus,
Let me drink from my cup.
"Written upon Reflection with Preface"
The old grain is exhausted,
The new grain not yet harvested,
Being quite aged as a farmer,
I encounter a year of disaster,
The days and months stretch long,
And troubles never cease.
The hope for a harvest,
Is already beyond reach,
The means for daily sustenance,
Barely suffice for cooking fire.
In the past ten days,
I've begun to feel hunger and want,
The year approaches its end,
With deep sighs, I reflect forever,
If I do not record this now,
How will later generations hear of it!
In youth, I faced family poverty,
In old age, I suffer prolonged hunger.
Beans and wheat are what I crave,
Who dares yearn for rich foods!
Hungry as in the time of nine meals,
In summer, I loathe winter clothes.
The year is nearing its end,
How full of toil and sorrow.
I often praise the porridge-giver's heart,
Deeply resent the one who covers his face.
Why begrudge the offer of food,
Only to perish in vain, leaving regrets.
Such excess was not their intent,
Standing firm in poverty has always been my goal.
Let hunger be as it may,
In the past, I had many teachers.
"Wax Day"
Wind and snow see off the remaining fate,
No hindrance, the season is already mild.
Plum and willow planted by the gate,
One branch bears lovely blossoms.
I sing, and you understand,
How much comfort in wine!
Unable to discern how much,
Zhāng Shān has a wondrous song.

"The Four Seasons"

Lush orchids beneath the window,
Dense willows before the hall.
When first we parted,
I did not think it would be long.
Traveling afar as a wanderer,
Midway, I met a fine friend.
Before speaking, hearts were intoxicated,
Not from sharing cups of wine.
Orchids withered, willows too declined,
Thus, these words were betrayed.
I thank the young men,
Whose friendship lacked sincerity.
Passion cost men their lives,

Two
I leave home at dawn in my carriage well-equipped,
Bound for Wúzhōng with purpose firm and equipped.
You ask what mission drives me now to roam—
It's neither trade nor martial deeds from home.
I've heard of Tián Zǐtài, a man renowned,
Whose righteous integrity in scholars abounded.
Though he has long passed from this mortal sphere,
His village still honors his legacy clear.
In life, he held a name above the rest,
In death, his fame eternally is blessed.
I won't emulate those who rush in vain,
Whose deeds last but a century's brief span.
Poem Three
In mid-spring, the timely rain does fall,
The first thunder rumbles from the east, enthral.
All dormant creatures stir in hidden fright,
Plants and trees stretch out in lush delight.
Gracefully, the newly arrived swallows fly,
In pairs, into my humble abode they hie.
Their former nest still stands in its old place,
Together they return to their nesting space.
Since we parted ways, time has passed by,
My courtyard grows wild, beneath the sky.
My heart remains steadfast, unlike a stone,
But what of your feelings, now you've flown?
Poem Four
Far-reaching, the hundred-foot tower high,
Clearly overlooks the four wastelands nigh.
At dusk, it becomes a home for returning clouds,
At dawn, a hall where flying birds enshrouds.
Mountains and rivers fill my view entire,
The vast plain alone stretches in mire.
Men of ancient times, seeking fame and might,
Passionately vied for this very site;
Once a hundred years have passed them by,
Together they return to Běimáng to lie.
Pine and cypress are felled by human hand,
High graves rise and fall across the land;
Crumbling foundations, no masters remain,
Where have the wandering souls gone, in vain?
Glory and splendor are truly precious, yes,
Yet they also evoke pity and distress!
Poem Five
In the east, there is a scholar, it's said,
Whose clothes are often tattered and thread.
In thirty days, he eats but nine meals,
In ten years, one hat his head reveals.
Hardship beyond compare he endures,
Yet his countenance always allures.
I wished to see this man, so I went,
At dawn, crossing rivers, on intent.
Green pines lined the road where they grew,
White clouds nestled by the eaves in view.
Knowing my purpose for coming here,
He took his qin and played it clear:
The upper strings startled the parting crane,
The lower strings sang of the lone phoenix's pain.
I wished to stay and live with you,
From now until the winter is through.
Poem Six
Lush and green, the valley's tree,
In winter and summer, constant as can be.
Year after year, it sees frost and snow,
Who says it doesn't the seasons know?
Tired of the world's empty chatter,
I sought friends in Línzī to matter;
At Jìxià, many debaters reside,
To resolve my doubts, I'd there confide.
Preparations made for the journey ahead,
I've bid my family farewell, as said.
Step by step, I halt at the door,
Sit back down, pondering once more.
Not that I mind the long road's length,
But fear being deceived of my strength;
If by chance it doesn't suit my mind,
Forever by the world, I'd be maligned.
These feelings are hard to fully convey,
So for you, I compose this poetic array.
Poem Seven
At dusk, the sky is cloudless and clear,
The spring breeze fans a gentle warmth near.
A beauty delights in the serene night,
Singing and reveling till dawn's light.
After singing, she heaves a long sigh,
Such scenes move people deeply, oh my.
Bright as the moon amidst the clouds white,
Radiant as blossoms in leaves' light,
How could they not have their moment fair?
But soon, what becomes of them, who'll care?
Poem Eight
In youth, robust and fierce was I,
Gripping my sword, alone I'd roam high.
Who says my travels were but near?
From Zhāngyè to Yōuzhōu, far and drear.
Hungry, I ate Shǒuyáng's fern so plain,
Thirsty, drank from Yì River's flow main.
No kindred spirits did I meet,
Only ancient mounds, somber and discreet.
By the roadside, two lofty graves stand,
Of Bó Yá and Zhuāng Zhōu, grand.
Such men are hard to find once more,
What else do I seek, in my core?
Poem Nine
I planted mulberries by the Yangtze's side,
Hoping in three years, they'd be harvested wide.
Just as the branches began to thrive,
Suddenly, mountains and rivers took a dive.
Leaves and twigs were broken and torn,
Roots and trunks in the blue sea were borne.
Spring silkworms have nothing to eat,
Who will provide for winter's heat?
Not planted on the plateau high,
What use is regret now, sigh?

"Twelve Miscellaneous Poems"
Human life has no root or stem,
Drifting like dust on a road's hem.
Scattered, turned by the wind's gust,
This form is no longer one to trust.
Since we land as brothers in this sphere,
Why must we be of kin so dear?
Find joy and make merry while you may,
Gather neighbors with wine to sway.
Prime years won't come back again,
Nor a second dawn after the rain;
Seize the time, strive with all your might,
For years and months wait for no one's plight.
Poem Two
The white sun sinks in the western stream,
The pale moon rises o'er the eastern gleam.
Far and wide, its radiance extends,
Vast and empty, the sky's scene transcends.
The wind enters through my chamber door,
At night, my pillow and mat feel cold to the core.
The air changes, I sense the season's shift,
Sleepless, I know the night's long drift.
I wish to speak, but none to share,
Raising my cup, I toast my shadow's care.
Sun and moon throw men aside,
Ambitions unfulfilled, nowhere to hide.
Thinking of this, my heart fills with grief,
Till dawn, I find no relief.
Poem Three
Glory and splendor are hard to retain,
Rise and fall cannot be measured or explained.
Once it was the lotus of spring's trio,
Now it's the autumn seedpod, oh.
Harsh frost binds the wild grasses tight,
Withered and gaunt, not yet out of sight.
Sun and moon cycle in their round,
But I depart, never to be rebound,
Longingly, I recall times of yore,
Remembering this breaks my heart sore.
Poem Four
A true man aims for all lands under the sky,
I wish to age without knowing why.
Kinfolk gathered together in one place,
Children and grandchildren in embrace.
Cups and strings enliven the morning sun,
Wine in the jar never seems undone.
Loosening my belt, I enjoy the cheer,
Rising late and sleeping early, without fear.
How unlike the scholars of today,
With hearts full of ice and charcoal's fray.
A hundred years, then to the grave we go,
Why cling to empty fame's hollow show!
Poem Five
I recall when I was young and strong,
Joyful even without a happy song.
Fierce ambitions soared beyond the seas,
Like wings yearning to fly with ease.
As years slipped away, my vigor declined,
This spirit gradually left my mind;
Encountering joy, I feel no delight,
Often burdened with worries day and night.
My strength slowly fades and wanes,
Each day feels weaker, it complains.
The ravine boat waits not a moment's stay,
Pulling me onward, no delay.
How much further lies the road ahead?
I know not where I'll rest my head.
The ancients cherished every inch of time,
Thinking of this fills me with dread sublime.
Poem Six
I recall the words of elders past,
Covering my ears, displeased I'd cast.
Yet how, in fifty years' swift flight,
I've witnessed this with my own sight.
The joys of my prime years I seek,
But not a trace remains, so bleak.
Time speeds away, turning afar,
This life won't double, like a star.
Spend all in revelry, make haste,
For years and months too quickly race.
Leave sons no gold, no hoarded store,
Why fret for what comes after more?
VII
Sun and moon won't slow their pace,
Seasons press in endless race.
Cold winds brush the barren boughs,
Fallen leaves cloak the long roads now.
My frail form with fate declines,
Dark locks early turned to signs.
White marks crown the human head,
The path ahead grows narrow, dread.
Home's but an inn for passing through,
I, a guest soon to bid adieu.
Where to go, this endless quest?
In Nánshān lies my final rest.
VIII
To farm for pay was not my hope,
My work lies in field and silk scope.
Hands-on, I've never ceased to toil,
Cold and hungry, on bran I broil.
Not aiming for a belly's fill,
Just wishing for fine grains to mill.
Coarse cloth suffices for winter's chill,
Rough hemp for summer's sun to still.
Yet even this I cannot gain,
Alas, such sorrow, such pain!
All others find their proper place,
My clumsy life has lost its grace.
What can one do with reason's plea?
Let me drink with Táo, wild and free.
IX
Far off on duties bound, I stray,
One heart torn between two ways.
Tears hidden, eastward I float,
Following the stream, time's fleeting note.
Sunset brings stars and Pleiades' light,
Fading behind the western height.
Desolate, worlds apart I stand,
Longing for meals in my homeland.
Passionate, I dream of south's return,
But the road's too far, no way to earn.
Barriers and bridges hard to cross,
In this piece, my message I toss.
X
Leisurely, I hold a wandering will,
Time flies, impossible to still.
Driven without a moment's rest,
Carriages speed to the east's crest.
Gloomy shades mimic musk's sweet scent,
Chill winds stir my heart's discontent.
Years and months have their constant course,
My stay here has prolonged by force.
Eagerly I recall close bonds of old,
Feelings long since left in the cold.
Slowly, ten years have passed me by,
Briefly tethered, I sigh.
Courts shaded by leftover trees,
Swiftly, sun and moon decrease.
XI
My journey hasn't been too far,
Looking back, bleak winds chill and mar.
Spring swallows rise with the season's call,
High flying, dust from beams they haul.
Border geese grieve, no place to stay,
Changing, they head north in array;
Parting swans cry in clear ponds deep,
Through summer's heat and autumn's sleep.
A sorrowful soul finds words hard to weave,
In the endless spring night, I grieve.
XII
Graceful, a sparrow on a pine high,
Lovely, a tender young child nearby.
Just fifteen years in age's span,
How can tall branches be his plan?
Nurturing hue with vital breath,
Radiant, a mind defying death.

Ode to the Impoverished Scholars, Seven Poems
All beings have their place to cling,
Lone cloud drifts with no comforting.
Dimly it vanishes in the air,
When will its fading light be there?
Dawn mist clears with morning's glow,
Flocks of birds together go;
A slow wing leaves the grove in sight,
Returning before the fall of night.
Measuring strength, I keep the old way,
Does it not bring cold and hunger's sway?
If no kindred soul remains,
What use is grief, what are the pains?
II
Bitter and sharp, the year draws to its end,
In coarse cloak, by the front porch, I spend.
Southern garden stripped of all its grace,
Northern yard with withered twigs embrace.
Empty jug, not a drop to pour,
Peek at the stove, no smoke to soar.
Poems and books pile by my seat,
Sun declining, no time to meet.
Leisure not as in Chén's plight,
Yet hidden grievances take flight.
What can console my heart's deep ache?
On ancient sages, my solace I take.
III
Old Róng with rope as belt, content,
Happily plucked his instrument;
Yuán Shēng in worn shoes, bare and poor,
Sang clear songs, his spirit pure.
Shùn's era long gone from our view,
Poor scholars in succession true.
Tattered robes don't cover the elbow's bend,
Wild herb soup, seldom a full blend.
Do I forget light furs to wear?
But ill-gained gains I cannot bear.
Cì, though eloquent in debate,
Could not my inner heart relate.
IV
Those content in poverty's state,
Since ancient times, like Qián Lóu great.
High titles do not tempt my pride,
Rich gifts I steadfastly deride.
Once life's span reaches its last breath,
Shabby clothes still cloak in death.
Don't I know the extreme of need?
But with the Way, no worries breed.
For a thousand years, it's been this way,
None like him since that distant day.
Born with benevolence at morn,
At dusk, death holds no cause to mourn.
V
Yuán Ān trapped in accumulated snow,
Aloof, untouched by worldly woe;
Ruǎn, when money came to hand,
That very day left his command.
Straw and fodder provide some warmth,
Picking greens for morning's forth.
Is it not truly hard and sore?
But hunger and cold are not the core.
Wealth and poverty in constant strife,
Triumph of Dao erases rife.
Supreme virtue crowns the land,
Pure integrity, a western stand.
VI
Zhòng Wèi loved his humble abode,
Weeds around his dwelling showed.
Secluded, cutting ties with all,
Writing poems, answering the call.
In all the world, none understood,
Save for one, Liú Gōng, who stood.
Why was this scholar so alone?
Truly, rare the like he'd known.
Steadfast, he found peace in his art,
Joy not in wealth or poor part.
Human affairs, I'm clumsy still,
Glad to follow his free will.
VII
Once Huáng Zǐlián, in days of yore,
Served a famed state, then closed the door.
One day he left his post behind,
In pure poverty, hard to find.
Famine moved his kind wife's heart,
Tears flowing, playing her part.
A man with will, though firm and true,
For children's sake, feels sorrow too.
Huì Sūn sighed in one meeting's span,
Generous gifts, he refused the plan.
Who says enduring need is hard?
Remote, those ancients set the guard.
Ode to the Two Hermits
The great cycle turns through the four seasons,
When their work is done, all things depart.
I ask, since the decline of the Zhōu dynasty,
How many have grasped this truth?
Looking around the Hàn court,
I see the two Shūs emulating this act.
With a lofty whistle, they return to their old abode,
Bowing deeply to the crown prince's tutor.
The entire court turned out to bid them farewell,
Their magnificent carriages filled the roads.
Parting brings sorrow to the heart,
But what are fleeting honors to care for?
Their deeds moved even passersby,
How worthy they were—not just ordinary praise!
Content with the joys of their neighborhood,
They pursued no trivial affairs.
Drawing their elders close on the mat,
They raised cups and spoke of simple things.
Inquiries about gold revealed their true hearts,
Clear words enlightened the unawakened.
Free in spirit, they delighted in their remaining years,
Unconcerned with worries beyond their lives.
Who says these men are gone?
With time, their Way shines brighter.
"Ode to the Three Good Men"
Donning caps, they rose to high posts,
Fearing only to be left behind by the times.
Diligently serving year after year,
Often worried their efforts were too slight.
Their loyal hearts, mistakenly revealed,
Made them the ruler's confidants.
Out, they accompanied his ornate carriage,
In, they attended by his crimson curtains;
Their admonitions were heeded,
Their counsel never found lacking.
Once their lord passed away,
They wished to follow him in death.
Deep gratitude is hard to forget,
How could they defy their sovereign's command?
At the tomb, they harbored no doubt,
Devoted to righteousness, their aspiration clear.
Thorns now cover the lofty mound,
The oriole's song is full of sorrow.
These good men cannot be ransomed back,
Tears fall freely, dampening my clothes.
"Ode to Jīng Kē"
Yān Dān knew how to nurture retainers,
Intent on avenging against mighty Qín.
He gathered a hundred brave men,
And at year's end, found Jīng Kē.
A gentleman dies for one who knows him,
Sword in hand, he left Yān's capital;
A white steed neighed on the broad road,
Fervently seeing him off.
His bristling hair lifted his tall cap,
Fierce energy filled his long tassels.
They drank farewell by the Yì River,
All seats filled with heroes.
Jiàn Lí played the mournful zhù,
Sòng Yì sang with a powerful voice.
The soughing sad wind passed,
Calm, cold waves arose.
The shāng note brought more tears,
The yǔ melody startled the brave.
Knowing he went never to return,
He would leave a name for ages.
Boarding the carriage, he never looked back,
Speeding under the canopy to Qín's court.
Swiftly traversing ten thousand miles,
Winding through a thousand cities.
The map unrolled, the plot unfolded,
The tyrant was struck with terror.
Alas, his sword skills were lacking,
So the great feat went unaccomplished!
Though the man is long gone,
After a thousand years, his spirit lingers.

"Reading the Classic of Mountains and Seas: Thirteen Poems"
In early summer, grass and trees grow tall,
Trees cluster lushly around my house.
All birds rejoice in having perches,
And I too love my humble home.
Having plowed and sown,
I return now and then to read my books.
My remote lane cuts off deep ruts,
Often turning old friends' carriages away.
Happily, I pour spring wine,
And pick vegetables from my garden.
A gentle rain comes from the east,
A good breeze accompanies it.
I browse through King Zhōu's legends,
And skim over the maps of mountains and seas.
In a glance, I traverse the universe—
If this isn't joy, what is?
Two
The jade terrace towers, radiant with clouds,
Queen Mother of the West wears a serene, lovely face.
She was born with heaven and earth,
No one knows how many years ago.
Her divine transformations are endless,
Her abodes are not confined to one mountain.
In high spirits, she sings new songs,
Far from the mundane words of the world.
Three
Far-reaching is the Huáijiāng Ridge,
Known as the Xuānpǔ Hill.
Gazing southwest toward Kūnlún's peaks,
Their radiant aura is beyond compare.
Tall and straight, luminous trees shine,
Clear jade-like waters flow freely.
I regret not joining King Mù of Zhōu,
To ride along on his journey there.
Four
Where does the red-wood tree grow?
It's on the sunny side of Mì Mountain.
Yellow flowers and crimson fruit,
Eating them prolongs one's life.
White jade congeals pure essence,
Fine gems emit wondrous light.
Not just treasures for gentlemen,
They were valued by Xuānyuán and Huángdì.
Five
Graceful are the three blue birds,
Their feathers strikingly beautiful.
By dawn, they serve as Queen Mother's envoys,
By dusk, they return to Sānwēi Mountain.
I wish to send word by these birds,
To convey to the Queen Mother:
"In this world, I desire little,
Only wine and longevity."
Six
Roaming freely on Wúgāo Heights,
I gaze distantly toward the Fúsāng Tree.
Its massive branches stretch millions of fathoms,
Lush and spreading, shading the Valley of Dawn.
Divine beings tend the cinnabar pool,
Bathing the sun each morning.
Once the sun's light ascends the sky,
What darkness remains unillumined?
Seven
Glistening are the three pearl trees,
Rooted in the shade of the Red River;
Stately cinnamon trees soar in the wind,
Eight trunks together form a grove.
Divine phoenixes dance on clouds,
Sacred luan birds harmonize with jade tones,
Though not treasures of the mortal world,
They win the Queen Mother's heart.
Eight
Since ancient times, all must die,
Who can attain eternal life?
Never dying, never aging,
Living millennia as if ordinary.
The Red Spring quenches my thirst,
Yuánqiū Hill provides ample grain.
Roaming with the sun, moon, and stars,
How could longevity ever cease?
Nine
Kuāfù conceived a grand ambition,
To race against the sun.
Both reached the abyss of Yúyuān,
Seemingly with no clear winner.
His divine strength was extraordinary,
How could draining rivers suffice him?
His legacy remains in the Dèng Forest,
His achievement realized after his death.
Ten
Jīngwèi carries tiny twigs,
To fill up the vast sea;
Xíngyāo dances with shield and axe,
His fierce will thus endures forever!
Since becoming one with nature, he has no regrets,
Transformed, he feels no remorse.
Yet his past resolve remains unfulfilled,
How can the right time ever be awaited?
Eleven
Chènwēi rampaged with cruel violence,
Qīnpī defied the Emperor's decree.
Yàyǔ, though forced to change,
Left Zǔjiāng to die alone.
Clearly, heaven above sees all,
Evil deeds must not be committed.
Long-lasting desolation is truly severe,
How can the jùn'è bird be relied upon?
Twelve
The owl sees the city walls,
In that state, scholars were exiled.
Thinking of the era of King Huái,
How often did it come to perch then?
On Qīngqiū there is a rare bird,
Claiming only it sees the truth.
Born for those who are lost,
Not to enlighten the nobleman.

Lofty and prominent in court and market,
Emperors must use talents with care.
Why were Gòng and Gǔn cast aside?
Because Chónghuá arose for this.
When Zhòngfǔ offered sincere advice,
Lord Jiāng became suspicious of him.
Nearing death, he spoke of thirst and hunger—

Three Poems
"Imitated Funeral Songs: Three Poems"
Where there is life, there must be death;
An early end isn't a shortened fate.
Last night we were all human together,
This morning, I'm on the ghost register.
Where has my soul's energy scattered to?
A withered form lodged in an empty coffin.
My beloved child cries, seeking his father;
Good friends stroke me and weep.
I no longer know gain or loss,
How can I perceive right and wrong?
A thousand autumns, ten thousand years hence,
Who will know glory or disgrace?
I only regret that while in the world,
I never drank enough wine.
In the past, I had no wine to drink,
Now the cup overflows, but I cannot partake.
Spring brew teems with floating bubbles,
When shall I taste it again?
Platters of food crowd before me,
Kin and old friends weep by my side.
I wish to speak, but my mouth has no voice;
I wish to see, but my eyes have no light.
Once I slept in the lofty hall,
Now I lodge in the wild grassland.
The wild grass knows no one's sleep,
Gazing afar, all is vast and boundless.
One morning I leave through the gate,
Never to return, not till the end of time.
How vast the wild grasslands are,
The white poplars rustle mournfully too.
In the harsh frost of the ninth month,
They send me off to the distant outskirts.
On all sides, no one dwells,
High graves stand rugged and steep.
The horse lifts its head and whinnies to the sky,
The wind itself sighs desolate.
Once the dark chamber is sealed shut,
A thousand years will not bring back the dawn.
A thousand years will not bring back the dawn,
Even the wise and virtuous can do nothing.
Those who came to see me off,
Each return to their own homes.
Relatives may retain some sorrow,
Others have already resumed their songs.
What is there to say about death?
My body entrusted to the mountain's embrace.
