Miscellaneous Writings
"The Peach Blossom Spring: Record and Poem"
During the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
A man of Wǔlíng made his living by fishing.
He followed a stream,
Forgetting the distance of the path.
Suddenly, he came upon a peach grove lining both banks,
For several hundred paces, no other trees,
Fragrant grass fresh and lovely,
Fallen petals swirling in profusion.
The fisherman found it very strange.
He went further ahead,
Wanting to reach the grove's end.
Where the grove ended at the water's source,
He found a mountain.
The mountain had a small opening,
Seemingly with a light within.
He left his boat and entered through the opening.
At first, it was very narrow,
Barely passable for a person.
After a few dozen steps more,
It suddenly opened up, broad and bright.
The land was level and vast,
Houses stood in neat rows.
There were fine fields, beautiful ponds, mulberries, bamboos, and the like.
Paths crisscrossed the fields,
The sounds of chickens and dogs intermingled.
People moved about, farming and working,
Men and women dressed just like outsiders.
The elderly and children
All appeared content and joyful.
Seeing the fisherman,
They were greatly surprised.
They asked where he had come from,
And he answered in detail.
They invited him to their home,
Setting out wine, killing a chicken for a meal.
The village heard of this person,
And all came to inquire.
They said their ancestors fled the turmoil of the Qín era,
Leading their families and fellow villagers
To this secluded place,
Never to leave again,
Thus cutting off contact with the outside world.
They asked what dynasty it was now,
Not knowing there had been a Hàn,
Let alone Wèi or Jìn.
The fisherman recounted all he knew,
And they sighed in amazement.
Others each invited him to their homes in turn,
All offering wine and food.
He stayed for several days,
Then took his leave.
The people there told him:
"It's not worth telling outsiders about this."
After he left,
He found his boat
And followed the old route back,
Marking it along the way.
Upon reaching the commandery,
He went to the prefect and reported this.
The prefect immediately sent men to follow him,
Seeking the marks he had made,
But they got lost and could not find the path again.
Liú Zǐjì of Nányáng,
A noble scholar,
Heard of this
And joyfully planned to go himself,
But did not succeed,
And soon fell ill and died.
After that, no one else sought the way.
The Yíng clan disrupted the cosmic order,
Wise men withdrew from that world.
Huáng and Qǐ went to Shāngshān,
These people also departed.
The traces of their going slowly faded and buried,
The path there became overgrown and abandoned.
They encouraged each other to farm diligently,
At sunset, they rested as they pleased.
Mulberries and bamboos cast ample shade,
Beans and millet sown in season.
Spring silkworms yielded long threads,
Autumn harvests owed no royal taxes.
Overgrown paths dimmed travel,
Cocks crowed and dogs barked in turn.
Ritual vessels followed ancient ways,
Clothing held no new designs.
Children sang freely as they roamed,
The grey-haired joyfully visited one another.
Grass in bloom marked the warm seasons,
Trees bare knew the harsh winds.
Though they had no calendar or records,
The four seasons made a year naturally.
Joyful and full of happiness,
Where was the need for cunning wisdom?
Their wondrous trace hidden for five hundred years,
One day revealed this divine realm.
Pure and shallow spring from different sources,
Soon it returned to seclusion.
Let me ask those who roam the worldly sphere:
How can you measure what's beyond the dust and noise?
I wish to tread on a light breeze,
Rise high to find my kindred spirit.
Rhapsody on Returning Home
"Rhapsody on Returning Home"
My family is poor,
and farming is insufficient to support ourselves.
With young children filling the house,
the jars have no stored grain,
and for the means to sustain life,
I see no method.
Relatives and friends often urged me to become a minor official,
and suddenly I felt inclined,
but there was no way to seek such a position.
It happened that there were affairs from all directions,
and the feudal lords valued kindness and benevolence,
while my uncle, knowing my poverty and hardship,
thus had me employed in a small town.
At that time, turmoil had not yet settled,
and I feared distant service,
but Péngzé was only a hundred lǐ from home,
and the benefits from the public fields
were enough to make wine,
so I sought the position.
After a few days,
I felt nostalgic and longed to return.
Why?
My nature is spontaneous,
not something that can be forced or restrained.
Though hunger and cold are pressing,
going against myself brings double suffering.
Whenever I engaged in worldly affairs,
it was all for the sake of my stomach, enslaving myself.
Thus, I felt disheartened and emotional,
deeply ashamed of my lifelong aspirations.
I still hoped for one harvest,
then to pack my clothes and leave by night.
Soon, my sister of the Chéng family died in Wǔchāng,
and in my eagerness to rush there,
I resigned from my post on my own.
From mid-autumn to winter,
I was in office for over eighty days.
Taking advantage of the situation to follow my heart,
I named this piece "Returning Home."
In the eleventh month of the yǐsì year.
Homeward I go, oh!
My fields and gardens will be overgrown—why not return?
Since I have let my mind be enslaved by my body,
Why should I mourn alone in disappointment?
I realize that the past cannot be remonstrated,
But know that the future can still be pursued;
Indeed, I have not gone far astray,
And feel that today is right while yesterday was wrong.
My boat sways lightly as it drifts afar,
The wind flutters, blowing my garments.
I ask a traveler about the road ahead,
Resenting the dimness of the dawn light.
Then I catch sight of my humble house,
Filled with joy, I hurry forward.
Servants welcome me,
My young children wait at the door.
The three paths are nearly overgrown,
But pines and chrysanthemums remain.
Leading the little ones indoors,
I find wine filling the jars.
Lifting the pot and cup, I pour myself a drink,
Gazing at the trees in the courtyard, my face brightens with pleasure.
Leaning by the south window, I indulge my pride,
Considering how easy it is to be content in this small space.
Daily strolls in the garden bring delight,
Though there is a gate, it is often closed.
Leaning on a staff, I wander and rest at will,
Sometimes raising my head to gaze into the distance.
Clouds drift aimlessly from the peaks,
Birds, weary of flight, know to return.
The sunlight dims, about to set,
I caress the lone pine, lingering.
Homeward I go, oh!
Let me cease all social ties and wanderings.
The world and I are at odds with each other,
What more is there to seek by driving out?
I delight in the heartfelt talks of kin,
And find joy in lute and books to dispel worries.
The farmers tell me spring has arrived,
There will be work in the western fields.
Sometimes I take a covered cart,
Sometimes I row a solitary boat.
Following winding paths through ravines,
And traversing rugged hills,
Trees flourish with vibrant growth,
Springs trickle as they begin to flow.
I admire how all things thrive in their season,
And lament that my life is nearing its end.
Enough, now!
How long shall I linger in this world?
Why not let my heart go as it pleases, whether to stay or leave?
Why rush about anxiously—where do I wish to go?
Wealth and honor are not my desires,
The realm of immortals is beyond hope.
I cherish fine days to wander alone,
Or, planting my staff, weed and tend the fields.
Climbing the eastern hill, I whistle long,
Facing the clear stream, I compose poems.
Let me follow nature's course to my end,
Rejoicing in Heaven's decree, what doubts remain?
"Biography of Master Five Willows"
No one knows where the master is from,
Nor are his surname and personal name known.
Beside his dwelling were five willow trees,
Hence, he took this as his nickname.
Quiet and reserved, he spoke little,
And did not covet glory or gain.
He loved reading books,
But did not seek deep understanding;
Whenever he grasped the meaning,
He would be so delighted as to forget eating.
By nature, he was fond of wine,
But being poor, he could not often obtain it.
Relatives and old friends, knowing this,
Would sometimes prepare wine and invite him.
When he went to drink, he would drain the cup,
Aiming surely to get drunk;
Once drunk, he would withdraw,
Never lingering reluctantly over staying or leaving.
His four walls stood bare and desolate,
Unable to shield him from wind and sun,
His coarse clothes were patched and mended,
His single bowl and gourd often empty,
Yet he remained content and at ease.
He often wrote essays to amuse himself,
Somewhat revealing his aspirations.
He forgot all gains and losses,
And thus lived out his life.
The Eulogy says:
Qián Lóu's wife once remarked:
'Not distressed by poverty and lowliness,
Not anxious for wealth and honor.'
Considering her words, was he not of their kind?
Drinking wine and composing poetry,
He delighted in his aspirations.
Was he a subject of the Wúhuái shì era?
Or of the Gětiān shì era?
Biography of Senior Official Mèng, Former Aide to the Great General Who Conquers the West of the Jìn Dynasty
"Biography of Senior Official Mèng, Former Aide to the Great General Who Conquers the West of the Jìn Dynasty"
The gentleman, named Jiā,
styled Wànnián,
was a native of È in Jiāngxià.
His great-grandfather Zōng
was renowned for his filial conduct
and served as a military commander in Wú.
His grandfather Jī
served as the governor of Lúlíng during the Yuánkāng era.
Zōng was buried in Xīnyáng County of Wǔchāng,
where his descendants settled,
thus becoming people of that county.
The gentleman lost his father young,
and lived with his mother and two younger brothers.
He married the tenth daughter of Táo Kǎn, the Duke Huán of Chángshā and Grand Marshal,
maintaining filial piety and fraternal love within the household,
which no one could disrupt,
earning praise from his local community.
Tranquil and reserved with profound tolerance,
by the age of twenty,
he was revered by his peers.
Guō Xùn of the same commandery,
known for his pure conduct,
was then considered superior to him.
Yet he often sighed in admiration of the gentleman's gentle elegance and balanced broad-mindedness,
feeling himself inadequate.
Xùn's cousin Lì,
also talented and ambitious,
shared equal fame with the gentleman at the time,
and always deferred to him with admiration.
Thus, his reputation topped the region,
and his fame spread to the capital.
Yǔ Liàng of Yǐngchuān, the Grand Commandant,
as the emperor's uncle and a figure of public esteem,
bore the heavy responsibility of a frontier post,
stationed in Wǔchāng,
and also governed Jiāngzhōu.
He appointed the gentleman as an assistant in the Lúlíng bureau.
Upon returning from an inspection tour of the commandery,
Liàng summoned him for an audience,
inquiring about local customs and governance.
He replied:
'I do not know,
you should ask the clerks upon my return.'
Liàng covered his mouth with a yak-tail whisk and laughed.
After the other assistants had left,
he called his younger brother Yì and told him:
'Mèng Jiā is truly a man of great virtue.'
The gentleman, having excused himself and stepped outside,
removed his official title on his own,
and walked home on foot.
His mother was in the hall,
and he joyfully reunited with his brothers,
harmonious and content.
After more than ten days,
he was reappointed as an educational affairs assistant.
At that time, Liàng was promoting the establishment of schools,
selecting Confucian officials with high standards,
and given the gentleman's reputation and integrity,
he was rightly chosen for this virtue-centered position.
Chǔ Bāo of Hénán, the Grand Tutor,
simple, solemn, and discerning,
then served as the governor of Yùzhāng.
He came to pay respects to Liàng,
and on New Year's Day, a grand gathering of regional officials was held,
mostly filled with eminent figures of the time.
The gentleman was seated quite far away.
Bāo asked Liàng:
'In Jiāngzhōu, there is a Mèng Jiā;
where is he now?'
Liàng said:
'He is among the attendees;
you may look for him yourself.'
Bāo scanned the crowd,
then pointed to the gentleman and said to Liàng:
'Could that be him?'
Liàng smiled joyfully,
pleased that Bāo had recognized him,
and impressed that the gentleman had caught Bāo's eye,
thus valuing him even more.
He was recommended as a Xiùcai,
and later served as a merit officer under Yǔ Yì, the General of Peaceful the West,
then successively as deputy of Jiāngzhōu, magistrate of Bāqiū, and military advisor to Huán Wēn, the Great General Conquering the West and Duke of Qiáo.
The gentleman's demeanor was gentle yet upright,
and Wēn held him in high regard.
On the ninth day of the ninth month,
Wēn excursioned to Lóngshān,
with all his staff gathered;
his four younger brothers and two nephews were also present.
At that time, the officials all wore military attire.
A gust of wind blew off the gentleman's hat,
and Wēn signaled to those around and the guests not to speak,
to observe his reaction.
The gentleman was initially unaware,
and after a while, he went to the restroom.
Wēn ordered the hat to be retrieved and returned to him.
Sūn Shèng of Tàiyuán, the Minister of Justice,
serving as a consulting military advisor,
was present at the time.
Wēn ordered paper and brush for him to compose a satire.
After finishing the text, it was shown to Wēn,
who placed it where the gentleman had been sitting.
When the gentleman returned,
he saw the satirical piece and requested a brush to reply,
without any hesitation,
his writing exceptionally outstanding,
earning the admiration of all present.
Sent on a mission to the capital,
he was appointed as a editorial郎 in the Imperial Secretariat,
but he declined the post.
Emperor Mù of the Xiàozōng period, hearing of his fame,
summoned him for an audience in the Eastern Hall.
The gentleman excused himself due to a foot ailment,
unable to perform the ceremonial bows.
An edict was issued to have him assisted inside.
He once served as deputy to Xiè Yǒng, the regional inspector,
Yǒng,
a native of Kuàijī,
passed away,
and the gentleman sought to attend to the duty of righteousness,
passing through Yǒngxīng on the route.
Xǔ Xún of Gāoyáng,
a man of outstanding talent,
who had renounced honors and refused office,
often wandered freely alone.
Residing as a guest within the county,
he once took a boat for a short trip,
and happened to meet the gentleman passing by.
He sighed and said:
'I know all the distinguished scholars of the capital,
yet I do not recognize this man.
I have only heard of a Mèng Jiā in Zhōngzhōu;
could it be him?
But how did he come here?'
He sent someone to inquire of the gentleman's attendants.
The gentleman told the messenger:
'I intended to visit,
but now I must first attend to my duty of righteousness;
I will return to see him soon.'
Upon his return,
he stayed for two nights;
they developed a profound mutual understanding,
as if they were old friends.
After returning to his post,
he was transferred to a central郎 position,
and soon promoted to chief of staff.
In court, he remained unassuming,
upholding integrity and compliance,
with no miscellaneous guests at his door.
Occasionally, when inspired by a sudden insight,
he would calmly order a carriage,
head straight to Lóngshān,
enjoy the scenery with hearty feasting,
and return only at dusk.
Wēn once casually remarked to him:
'One cannot be without authority;
that is how I can command you.'
Later, he passed away at home due to illness,
at the age of fifty-one.
From his youth
until the age of fifty,
he never acted in improper compliance,
nor spoke with boastful pride,
and never showed expressions of joy or anger.
He loved drinking to the full,
yet remained composed even when exceeding limits.
When indulging in his carefree satisfaction,
he would blend into the distance with a harmonious spirit,
as if no one else was around.
Wēn once asked him:
'What is so good about wine,
that you are so fond of it?'
The gentleman smiled and replied:
'You, sir, simply do not grasp the delight within wine.'
When asked about listening to musicians,
why strings are not as good as bamboo,
and bamboo not as good as voice,
he answered:
'Because it draws closer to nature.'
Luó Hán of Guìyáng, a Grand Master of the Palace,
composed a verse about him:
'Mèng Shēng excels in joyful drinking,
without straying from his intent.'
Liú Dān of Nányáng, a Grand Master of the Palace,
had previously served with the gentleman in Wēn's office.
Yuānmíng's paternal uncle, the Minister of Ceremonies Kuí, once asked Dān:
'If he were still alive,
would he have become a high minister by now?'
Dān replied:
'He was originally fit for the highest offices.'
Such was the esteem in which he was held at the time.
Yuānmíng's mother
was the gentleman's fourth daughter.
Thoughts of maternal kindness and filial duty
profoundly moved his heart.
Carefully compiling records of his deeds,
I have written this biography.
Fearing any inaccuracies
that might tarnish the virtue of a noble gentleman,
I have proceeded with caution as if treading on thin ice.
Eulogy says:
Confucius stated:
'Cultivate virtue and refine one's work,
so as to act timely.'
When a gentleman remains pure in a humble gate,
his fine reputation shines brightly;
when he serves in the court with official cap,
his virtuous words truly gather respect.
The Way is eternal but fate is short,
unable to complete the grand endeavor,
alas, how regrettable!
The benevolent are bound to live long—
how could this saying be mistaken!
Nine Chapters Composed While Reading History
I have composed these after being moved while reading Records of the Grand Historian.
Yí Qí
"Yí Qí"
The two men yielded the state,
together going to the seaside.
Heaven and man brought revolution,
they dwelled in seclusion, cutting off traces.
Picking ferns, singing loudly,
yearning for the age of Huángdì and Yú.
Upright winds transcended customs,
thus moving even the timid.
"Jīzǐ"
The feeling of leaving home
still brings lingering steps.
How much more at dynastic change,
touching everything, all seems wrong.
Sorrowful Jīzǐ,
how could his heart be at peace?
The song of the cunning boy,
how mournful and sad.
"Guǎn Bào"
Knowing others is not easy,
mutual understanding truly hard.
Sweetness in new friendship,
shatters when profit turns cold.
Guǎn Zhòng followed his heart,
Bào Shū surely felt at ease.
Rare affection shone in both,
their fine names remained intact.
"Chéng Chǔ"
Sacrificing life is truly hard,
a scholar dies for one who knows him.
Seeing righteousness, they went to meet it,
truly these two men.
Chéng Yīng raised his sword,
fearing the lingering shame.
Their virtuous deeds forever known,
recorded through a hundred generations.
"Seventy-Two Disciples"
Reverent at the Rain Dance Altar,
none were not worthy.
All reflected sun and moon,
sharing the ultimate teachings.
Grief springs from rarity of talent,
emotion stirred by deep attachment.
Yán Huí died early,
while Zìgòng alone lived long.
"Qū Jiǎ"
Cultivate virtue and refine one's work,
striving to act timely.
Like those Jì and Xiè,
who wouldn't aspire to this?
Alas, these two worthies,
met with much doubt in their time.
Waiting, gazing, expressing will,
moved by the owl, offering words.
"Hán Fēi"
The lush fox hides in its cave,
yet by its fur brings self-harm.
A gentleman missing his time,
grows old guarding gates.
Cunning actions invite disaster,
contentious speech summons trouble.
Mournful Master Hán,
ultimately died from "Shuì Nán".
Two Scholars of Lǔ
"Two Scholars of Lǔ"
Changing dynasties, following the times,
confused by change is foolish.
Steadfast these men,
specially maintained integrity.
Virtue not lasting a hundred years,
they felt our poetry and books defiled.
They left without looking back,
clad in coarse clothes, dwelling in seclusion.
Zhǎnggōng Zhāng
"Zhǎnggōng Zhāng"
How far-sighted, Zhǎnggōng,
aloof, for what reason?
Worldly paths are manifold,
all differed from his own.
Drawing reins, he came and went,
alone nurturing his will.
Concealing his traces year after year,
who understood his intent?
"Rhapsody on Scholars Not Meeting Their Time, with Preface"
Formerly Dǒng Zhòngshū wrote "Rhapsody on Scholars Not Meeting Their Time",
and Sīmǎ Zǐcháng also composed one.
I have often, on days of leisure from three activities,
in spare moments from study,
read their writings,
and sighed with profound melancholy.
To tread in trust and think of obedience
is the good conduct of living men;
to embrace simplicity and guard tranquility
is the sincere nature of gentlemen.
Since the genuine wind was said to have passed,
great artifice has arisen;
neighborhoods slacken in integrity and retiring virtue,
courts and markets drive ambitions for easy advancement.
Men who cherish uprightness and aspire to the Way
may hide their jade-like qualities in their prime;
those with pure selves and clean conduct
may pass their lives in vain toil.
Thus Yí Qí and the Hermits sighed about where to find peace,
and Sānlǘ gave voice to his despairing lament.
How sorrowful!
To dwell in bodily form for a hundred years,
yet vanish in the blink of an eye;
the difficulty of establishing one's conduct,
with not even a city's reward.
This is why the ancients took up brush with fervent emotion,
repeatedly expressing what could not be restrained.
To convey and express one's spirit,
is it not only through writing?
Stroking the scroll, I hesitate and ponder,
then, moved, compose this rhapsody.
I inquire of the great mass that receives breath—
Why is humankind alone endowed with spirit?
Endowed with divine wisdom and inner light,
They uphold the Three and Five to leave a name.
Some beat the soil in self-contentment,
Others greatly aid the common people;
Neither diving nor soaring is undue,
Often proudly acting as their feelings dictate.
The world drifts along and thus passes away,
Things divide into groups and contrast each other.
Dense nets are set, and fish take fright,
Vast snares are laid, and birds are alarmed.
Those enlightened ones, wise and perceptive,
Flee from official salaries to return to farming.
Mountains stand tall, embracing shadows,
Rivers stretch wide, concealing sounds.
Gazing toward Xuānyuán and Tángyáo, they sigh forever,
Content with poverty and lowliness, renouncing glory.
The pure source flows and divides long ago,
Beauty and ugliness arise and take different paths.
Considering the value of all conducts,
None is more delightful than doing good.
Revering the supreme mandate of Heaven,
Following the sages' surviving texts.
Express loyalty and filial piety to ruler and parents,
Cultivate trust and righteousness in the village lanes.
With sincere hearts, they gain renown,
Not feigning actions to seek praise.
Alas!
The crowd echoes in slandering the different,
Things detest those above them;
The profoundly wise are called deluded,
The straightforward are deemed absurd.
Open and utterly fair, free of suspicion,
Yet end up shamed and slandered.
Though holding jade and orchids in hand,
Their fragrance and purity—who appreciates them?
How sorrowful!
That scholars meet no recognition,
No longer in the ages of Yándì and Dìkuí.
Alone, I cultivate myself with diligence,
How could the triple self-reflection be neglected?
Hoping to advance in virtue timely,
But when the time comes, fortune does not favor.
Without the wise words of Yuán Shēng,
I think of Zhāng Jì, ultimately obscured;
Sympathize with Féng the elder in a low post,
Relying on the Wèi governor to adopt his plan.
Though barely recognized as perceptive,
He suffered bitterly and wasted years.
Consider how the market had no tiger,
Yet three men's tales could deceive.
Mourn for the brilliance of Jiǎ Fù,
Reining his distant steed in narrow bounds.
Lament the profound depth of Dǒng the minister,
Repeatedly facing peril, barely escaping.
Moved by the sage's lack of a match,
Tears stream down, soaking my sleeves.
Receiving the clear teachings of former kings,
Which say the Way of Heaven favors none;
Purified, it uses the One as a mirror,
Constantly aiding the good and protecting the benevolent.
Yet Bó Yí starved in old age,
Yán Huí died young and in poverty;
Grieved by his plea for a carriage to buy an outer coffin,
Saddened by those eating ferns, then perishing;
Though devoted to learning and righteous deeds,
Why such bitterness in life and death!
Doubting if virtue's reward is thus,
I fear these words are but empty claims.
Why, across vast ages, there's no lack of talent,
But rarely a path not blocked.
Those ancients, full of fervor,
Ailed that their remarkable names went unestablished.
Lǐ Guǎng devoted his youth to governance,
Deserving reward of ten thousand towns;
Yet his lofty will bowed to petty men,
Not even a foot of land was granted.
Leaving sincerity and trust after his death,
He moved the masses to mournful tears.
Shāng Yāng exhaustively planned to save the state,
His words initially heeded, then disaster struck.
Why do fair moments so easily fade?
Why does harming the superior rush so urgently?
The azure heavens are remote and vast,
Human affairs never cease.
Some perceive, some remain in darkness,
Who can fathom their principles?
Rather steadfast in poverty to fulfill my will,
Than compromise and burden myself.
Since high chariots and caps are not glory,
How can a coarse robe be shame?
Truly, by mistaken encounters I gain clumsiness,
Yet joyfully I return and cease.
Holding my solitary ideals to end my years,
Declining high prices in court and market.
"Rhapsody on Quieting the Passions"
Originally, Zhāng Héng wrote "Rhapsody on Settling the Passions,"
Cài Yōng wrote "Rhapsody on Calming the Passions,"
They restrained wanton expressions and upheld tranquility,
Beginning with unrestrained thoughts,
But ending in quiet correctness.
Aiming to curb wandering, wayward hearts,
Indeed, they aid in admonition.
Literary men,
Through successive generations, continued the work,
Each drawing on related themes,
Expanding the language and meaning.
With much leisure in my garden and lodge,
I again took up the brush to write one.
Though lacking in literary excellence,
I hope not to betray the authors' intent.
How I cherish her graceful, transcendent beauty,
Alone outstanding in this world, excelling the crowd.
She displays a beauty that could topple cities,
Hoping her virtue will be known through hearsay.
She wears tinkling jade to match her purity,
And vies in fragrance with secluded orchids;
Her gentle feelings remain aloof from vulgarity,
Her noble aspirations soar high as the clouds.
I grieve that dawn's light so easily turns to dusk,
And lament the long toil of human life.
All meet the same end within a hundred years,
Why so little joy and such abundant sorrow?
She lifts the crimson curtain and sits upright,
Playing the clear zither for her own delight;
Her slender fingers send forth lingering charm,
She lifts her white sleeves in fluttering elegance.
Her beautiful eyes glance with a sparkling gaze,
Holding speech and smile indistinguishably.
As the melody reaches its midpoint,
The sunlight falls on the western eaves.
The sad autumn wind rustles the woods,
White clouds cling to the mountains.
Looking up, I gaze at the heavenly path,
Looking down, she briskly plucks the singing strings.
Her divine demeanor is charming and lovely,
Her every movement graceful and refined.
Stirred by her pure music that moves me,
I long to sit knee-to-knee and converse.
I wish to go to her and pledge my vow,
But fear breaching propriety would be a fault.
Waiting for the phoenix to convey my words,
I worry others might precede me.
My heart is anxious and finds no peace,
My soul flits restlessly in moments.
I wish to be the collar on her robe,
To catch the lingering fragrance from her fair head;
But grieve that the silken gown is removed at night,
Regretting the autumn night seems endless.
I wish to be the sash on her skirt,
To gird her slender, graceful waist;
But sigh that warmth and coolness change with seasons,
And she may discard the old for new attire.
I wish to be the gloss in her hair,
Sweeping over her dark locks on sloping shoulders;
But mourn that the fair one often washes,
Leaving me to dry and wither in plain water.
I wish to be the kohl on her brows,
Following her gaze in graceful arches;
But lament that cosmetics stay fresh,
And I might be removed for splendid makeup.
I wish to be the mat of reeds,
Cradling her delicate form in autumn;
But grieve that patterned blankets replace me in use,
Only to be sought again after a year.
I wish to be the silk in her shoes,
Encircling her plain feet in their movements;
But mourn that her comings and goings have their times,
Leaving me cast aside before the bed.
I wish to be her shadow in the day,
Always following her form east and west;
But grieve that tall trees cast much shade,
Regretting sometimes we cannot be together.
I wish to be the candle in the night,
Illuminating her jade face between the pillars;
But mourn the rising sun's spreading light,
Suddenly extinguishing my glow and hiding my brightness.
I wish to be the bamboo fan,
Held in her soft grip to stir cool breezes;
But grieve at the morning fall of white dew,
Looking at sleeves and collar, distant and remote.
I wish to be the paulownia tree,
Made into a singing zither on her lap;
But mourn that joy at its peak brings sorrow,
And she finally pushes me away, ceasing the music.
Reflecting on these wishes, all are thwarted,
Vainly binding myself with bitter longing.
Holding weary emotions with no one to tell,
I wander aimlessly in the southern woods.
Resting where orchids retain leftover dew,
Sheltering under the lingering shade of green pines.
Joy and fear mingle in my heart.
In the end, solitude and no sight of her,
Alone, tormented by thoughts, I search in vain.
Gathering my light robe, I return to the path,
Gazing at the setting sun with flowing sighs.
Pacing hesitantly, I forget my way,
My expression sorrowful and strained.
Leaves rustle as they leave the branches,
The air turns chill and cold sets in.
The sun, with its shadow, sinks together,
The moon casts lovely scenes atop the clouds.
Birds return alone with mournful cries,
Beasts seek mates but do not return.
Mourning that my prime years are late in dusk,
Regretting this year is about to end.
Hoping to follow her in night dreams,
My spirit flutters, unsettled.
Like a boat that has lost its oar,
Or climbing a cliff with nothing to grasp.
At this time, the Pleiades fill the window,
The northern wind blows bleakly.
Restless, unable to sleep,
Countless thoughts linger in my mind.
Rising to adjust my belt, awaiting dawn,
Thick frost glitters on the white steps.
Roosters fold their wings, not yet crowing,
A flute's distant sound flows clear and sorrowful,
Beginning subtle, serene, and harmonious,
Ending vast and bright, yet heart-wrenching.
Imagining my beloved is here,
I entrust my feelings to the passing clouds.
The clouds drift away without a word,
Time swiftly passes by.
Vainly I toil in thought, grieving alone,
Ultimately blocked by mountains and girded by rivers.
Facing the clear breeze to dispel my burdens,
I entrust my weak will to the returning waves.
Disapproving of meetings like spreading weeds,
I recite the remaining songs of Shàonán.
Setting aside all worries to preserve sincerity,
I let my distant feelings rest in the eight far reaches.
"Eulogy on the Filial Piety of Sons of Heaven"
Yú Shùn, Xià Yǔ, Yīn Gāozōng, Zhōu Wénwáng.
Yú Shùn's father was obstinate, his mother deceitful,
Yet he served them in the fields,
With increasingly sincere filial piety,
Thus Yáo heard of it and entrusted the throne to him.
Though he possessed the wealth of the world,
And was honored as the Son of Heaven,
He felt that if he did not please his parents,
It was like being destitute with nowhere to return.
Only by obeying his parents could he find satisfaction,
If he neglected them even briefly,
It was like an infant's longing,
Hence it is said Shùn was devoted even at fifty.
The "Shū" says:
"Strike the sounding stone,
Drum the zithers and lutes while singing,
The ancestral spirits will come."
This means thinking of their coming to instruct.
Love and reverence exhausted in serving parents,
Thus his virtuous teachings extended to the common people,
And served as a model throughout the land.
When Xià Yǔ possessed the world,
He served the ancestral temple,
Yet he himself lived frugally,
To deepen his filial piety.
Confucius said:
"As for Yǔ,
I find no fault with him.
He ate and drank meagerly but showed utmost filial piety to spirits,
Wore coarse clothes but made ceremonial robes beautiful."
Yǔ's virtue was thus praised and known.
The virtue of a sage,
Cannot surpass filial piety and reverence,
The way of filial piety and reverence,
Has no greater beauty.
Yīn Gāozōng observed the mourning hut,
Remaining silent for three years,
All officials governed themselves and listened to the prime minister,
After three years he spoke again,
And all under heaven rejoiced,
Virtuous teachings greatly prevailed,
And the Yīn dynasty thereby flourished.
The "Shī" says:
"When one man has blessings,
Millions of people rely on him."
Is this not referring to him?
When Zhōu Wénwáng was crown prince,
He attended upon his father Wáng Jì thrice daily,
At cockcrow, he went to the bedroom door,
Asked the inner attendant,
If the attendant said "Well,"
Wénwáng would be pleased;
If "Unwell,"
He would look worried,
And could not walk steadily.
At noon and evening,
It was the same.
When food was served,
He always checked if it was warm or cool appropriately;
After the meal,
He asked what was eaten before withdrawing.
Wénwáng's filial way was greatly illustrious,
His influence spread from near to far,
Setting an example for his own wife,
To extend to the family and state,
Thus he won the joyful hearts of all states,
To serve his former kings.
Eulogy says:
How perfect is the queen's virtue,
Sagely reverence comes from Heaven.
Engaging in pottery and fishing to provide sustenance,
She humbly offered sacrifices to ancestors.
Grieving at her parents' illness with worried countenance,
She observed silence during mourning.
When the sovereign has blessings,
A thousand generations rely thereon.
"Eulogy for Biographies of Filial Piety Among Feudal Lords"
Zhōu Gōng Dàn, Lǔ Xiào Gōng, Héjiān Huì Wáng.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn
was the younger brother of King Wǔ.
When King Chéng was young,
Zhōu Gōng acted as regent,
establishing rituals and creating music,
sacrificing to Hòu Jì at the suburban altar to match Heaven,
and worshipping King Wén in the Bright Hall,
to match the Supreme Deity.
Thus, within the four seas,
each came according to their duties to sacrifice.
The Book of Songs says:
"Oh, solemn and pure temple,
reverent and harmonious are the illustrious assistants."
This means the feudal lords delighted in their positions and respected their duties.
Zhòngní said:
"Nothing is greater in filial piety than revering one's father,
and nothing greater in revering one's father than matching Heaven."
Then Zhōu Gōng was such a man,
noble but not arrogant,
the higher his position, the more humble he became,
inheriting the glorious achievements of Wén and Wǔ,
his filial piety connecting with the divine,
his light covering the four seas.
King Wǔ enfeoffed him in Lǔ,
providing complete rituals and music,
to serve the ancestral temple.
When Lǔ Xiào Gōng was a prince,
King Xuān of Zhōu asked which prince could guide and instruct the feudal lords to establish him.
Fán Mùzhòng praised his filial piety, saying:
"Solemnly revering the bright spirits,
and respectfully serving the elderly,
in assigning duties and administering punishments,
he would always consult the inherited teachings,
seek advice from past precedents,
not transgressing what was inquired,
not violating what was consulted."
The King said:
"Then he can instruct and govern his people."
Thereupon he was appointed at the Yí Palace,
and became Xiào Gōng.
Showing reverence in the ancestral temple,
means not forgetting one's parents;
is it not fitting for one who possesses a state!
Hàn Héjiān Huì Wáng
was the great-grandson of Xiàn Wáng.
Among the feudal lords of the Western Capital,
many had the fault of arrogance and licentiousness,
but those renowned for virtue
included only Xiàn Wáng,
and Huì Wáng succeeded him.
The Book of Hàn praises him for being able to cultivate Xiàn Wáng's conduct.
When his mother passed away,
he observed mourning with full ritual.
Emperor Āi issued an edict commending him,
considering him a model for the imperial clan,
and increased his fief by ten thousand households.
According to ritual,
the ancients all did thus;
as for the decadent customs of later times,
he was truly worthy,
for it is difficult to be noble yet follow ritual.
That he received praise and reward
was indeed fitting.
Eulogy says:
Nobility and arrogance take different paths,
yet meet unexpectedly.
Zhōu Gōng toiled with humility,
thus achieving greatness and radiance.
The two lords succeeding in Lǔ,
followed frugality and avoided excess.
Héjiān adhered to ritual,
the Hàn clan relied thereon.
"Eulogy for Biographies of Filial Piety Among Ministers and Great Officers"
Kǒngzǐ, Mèng Zhuāngzǐ, Yǐng Kǎoshū.
Kǒngzǐ
was a man of Lǔ.
At home he served his father and elder brothers,
abroad he served the lords and ministers,
in funeral matters he dared not be unconscientious,
thus it is said:
"Filial, oh filial piety,
friendly with brothers,
this too is governing."
When the ruler bestowed raw meat,
he would always cook it and offer it to ancestors,
even with simple food he fasted,
sacrificing as if ancestors were present.
When villagers performed exorcism,
he stood in court robes at the eastern steps,
the ultimate in filial piety.
The highest virtue and essential way,
nothing is greater than filial piety,
thus Zēng Shēn received and recorded it.
Disciples like Zǐyóu and Zǐxià
often consulted and received instruction from him.
Xǔ Zhǐ not tasting medicine
was recorded as patricide.
Zǎi Wǒ briefly suggesting reducing mourning
was reproached for inhumanity.
His words matched the canonical teachings,
his deeds matched worldly models.
His virtue and righteousness were worthy of honor,
his actions worthy of emulation,
his legacy enduring,
his fame spreading for millennia.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ
was a man of Lǔ.
Kǒngzǐ praised his filial piety,
saying other things he could do,
but not changing his father's governance,
and keeping his father's ministers,
this was truly difficult.
For a filial son serving his parents,
serves the deceased as if they were alive;
thus when there is injustice he should dispute it,
but what was not disputed while they lived,
should not be changed after their death.
Not changing the father's way for three years
is still called filial,
how much more for a lifetime!
Yǐng Kǎoshū
was a man of Zhèng.
Duke Zhuāng, because of Shū Duàn,
swore to his mother:
"Not until the Yellow Springs,
shall we meet again."
Later he regretted it.
Kǎoshū was a border official,
heard of this,
and had a presentation for the Duke.
The Duke bestowed food on him,
but he set aside the meat.
The Duke asked him,
and he replied:
"This humble person has a mother
who has never tasted your lordship's stew,
may I give this to her?"
The Duke said:
"You have a mother to give to,
but I alone have none!"
Kǎoshū said:
"What do you mean?"
The Duke told him the reason,
and confessed his regret.
Kǎoshū said:
"If you dig the earth until reaching springs,
and meet in a tunnel,
who would say this is not so?"
The Duke followed this,
and thus mother and son were as before.
The gentleman says:
Yǐng Kǎoshū
was of pure filial piety,
loving his mother and extending this to Duke Zhuāng.
The Book of Songs says:
"The filial son never fails,
forever he gives to your kind."
This refers to this indeed.
Eulogy says:
Benevolence roots in fraternal duty,
sagehood too bases on filial piety.
Reverent was Master Ni,
truly made by Heaven.
The two sons served their parents,
following ritual and heeding instructions.
Eternal bestowal of pure virtue,
not changing inherited conduct.
"Eulogy for Biographies of Filial Piety Among Scholars"
Gāo Chái,
was a man of Wèi.
When he lost his parents,
he wept tears of blood for three years,
never showing his teeth,
which is called weeping without restraint,
and speaking without adornment.
As the magistrate of Wǔchéng, his transformative influence spread,
causing those among the people who had not served their parents well to reform,
and to conduct mourning according to ritual.
The virtue of a nobleman is like the wind;
by taking the lead with his own person,
the people did not neglect their parents.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn,
was a man of Lǔ.
He injured his foot while descending the hall,
and after it healed,
he did not go out for several months,
still wearing a worried expression.
He said:
"I heard from Zēngzǐ that
parents give us life whole,
and we should return ourselves to them whole;
this can be called filial piety.
Therefore, a nobleman, with every step he takes,
every word he speaks,
dares not forget his parents,
dares not inflict injury or damage;
this is the beginning of filial piety."
Those who can be so reverent and cautious,
yet still encounter disaster and hardship,
have never existed.
Kǒng Fèn,
was a man of Fúfēng.
In his youth, he was renowned in his prefecture for his filial conduct,
providing for his parents with utmost care.
While in office,
only his mother enjoyed the sweetest and finest foods,
while his wife and children ate vegetables.
He held positions with purity throughout.
Human nature desires to treat one's parents generously,
yet there are also limits;
extravagance is difficult to sustain,
and those who can practice frugality to fully provide are
rare.
Huáng Xiāng,
was a man of Jiāngxià.
At nine years old, he lost his mother,
and his longing for her made him gaunt to the bone.
He served his father with all his strength to provide for him,
going without quilt or trousers in winter to ensure his father had all delicacies,
fanning his bed and pillow in summer,
and warming the mat with his own body in cold weather.
Emperor Hé of Hàn praised him,
granting him special and extraordinary gifts.
Throughout his official posts, he was respectful and diligent,
his favor and emoluments bringing honor to his parents,
truly one who "rose early and retired late,
not disgracing those who gave you birth."
The Eulogy says:
Illustrious and sincere, these many gentlemen,
their deeds differed but their renown was equal.
All could toil day and night,
to honor their parents through righteousness.
Leading their cities,
they transformed their people.
Loyalty to enlighten their rulers,
their filial piety was pure.
"Eulogy on Biographies of Filial Commoners"
Jiāng Gé, Lián Fàn, Rǔ Yù, Yīn Táo.
Jiāng Gé,
was a man of Qí.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
he fled from bandits carrying his mother on his back.
The bandits, admiring his virtue,
spared him and showed him the way to safety.
He toiled as a laborer to repay debts,
to provide sweet and warm provisions,
with a gentle countenance and cheerful demeanor,
to bring his mother utmost joy,
desiring her comfort,
he pulled the cart himself to travel.
The villagers revered him,
calling him Jiāng the Greatly Filial.
He rose to the position of Commandant of the Five Guards,
and the emperor praised him,
bestowing upon him great favor and待遇.
When he requested to retire,
an imperial edict commended and honored him,
honoring him at his home for life,
to highlight his extraordinary conduct.
Lián Fàn,
was a man of Jīngzhào.
Orphaned young,
at fifteen, he went to Shǔ,
to retrieve his father's remains.
Encountering a stone boat that capsized,
Fàn clung to the bones and sank,
but boatmen rescued him,
barely escaping death,
and thus he brought the remains back.
Later, in office, he saved the governor from danger,
serving his former superior with full loyalty.
During Emperor Zhāng's time, he served as a governor,
and the people sang his praises.
Filial piety is
the root of humanity,
the source from which teaching arises.
Thus, Fàn was brave in facing danger,
benevolent in governing the people,
able to manifest righteousness.
Rǔ Yù,
was a man of Chénjùn.
At five years old,
when his mother fell ill and could not eat,
Yù also refused to eat.
His mother, pitying him,
forced herself to eat.
Yù could discern her condition,
knowing she was ill,
and would again refuse to eat.
His clansmen called him the "Extraordinary Child."
At fifteen,
he was renowned in his hometown.
When his parents passed away,
his longing led him to emaciation,
and he gave his wealth to his brothers,
retreating to live in the marshes,
which noblemen considered difficult.
Moreover, his filial piety as a young child was natural,
truly a matter of innate character.
Yīn Táo,
was a man of Rǔnán.
At twelve years old,
he was noted for his filial piety.
When his father passed away,
his emotions were in accord with ritual.
A long snake appeared at his gate,
and the whole family fled,
but Táo, because the funeral coffin was there,
remained alone in the hut unmoved.
Relatives tried to persuade and lead him away,
but none could move him,
and he cried out even more loudly.
Thus, he became famous,
and repeatedly declined official appointments.
The wise are not perplexed,
the brave do not fear;
Táo's filial piety towards his parents,
with wisdom and courage both evident at a tender age,
is indeed remarkable.
The Eulogy says:
Serving parents to bring them joy,
the difficulty lies in one's demeanor.
Some provide with official salary,
I provide with labor.
Righteousness lies in love and respect,
honor requires no pretense.
Oh, you multitude of commoners,
take these former models as your mirror.
"Eulogy on the Fan Painting"
The Old Man with the Bamboo Staff, Cháng Jū and Jié Nì, Yúlíng Zhòngzǐ, Zhāng Chánggōng, Bǐng Mànróng, Zhèng Cìdū, Xuē Mèngcháng, Zhōuyáng Guī.
The ways of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors are distant,
their pure customs daily fade.
The nine schools of thought are uneven,
mutually pushing and toppling.
Forms chase after things and shift,
the mind lacks constant standards.
Thus, enlightened individuals,
sometimes choose seclusion.
Not toiling with four limbs,
not distinguishing the five grains.
The transcendent elder,
day and evening tends the fields.
The far-off Jǔ and Nì,
delight in plowing together.
Birds do not startle at their approach,
they mingle with herds of beasts.
Supreme is Yúlíng,
nourishing a vast spirit.
Disdaining those with teams of four horses,
content with tending his garden.
Once Zhāng Shēng took office,
but had to return due to matters.
Considering my inability,
I loftily decline the human world.
Lofty Bǐng Gōng,
seeing the cliff, turns back.
Neither arrogant nor stingy,
the road ahead is perilous.
Old man Zhèng found no meeting of minds,
fishes by the riverbank.
Drinking together beneath the trees,
discussing profound subtleties.
Mèng Cháng traveled for learning,
when heaven's net was sometimes loose.
Thinking of my wise friends,
I shake my coarse cloth and go with them.
How admirable is Master Zhōu,
claiming illness to live in leisure.
His heart set on purity and nobility,
carefree and self-content.
Secluded is the humble gate,
abundant the flowing stream.
With lute and books,
looking around, I have companions.
Having drunk from the river, I am satisfied,
all else beyond is unnecessary.
Reflecting on a thousand years,
entrusting my bond to solitary wanderings.
"Admonition to My Sons Yǎn et al."
To Yǎn, Sì, Bīn, Yì, and Tóng:
Heaven and earth endow life,
birth inevitably leads to death.
Since ancient times, sages and worthies,
who could avoid this alone?
Zǐxià once said:
'Death and life are destined,
wealth and honor lie with heaven.'
Among the four friends,
those who personally received his teachings,
uttered these words,
was it not because failure and success cannot be recklessly sought,
and longevity or premature death never have external petitions?
I am over fifty years old,
poor and bitter since youth,
often due to family hardship,
wandered east and west.
By nature firm but talent clumsy,
often at odds with the world.
Considering it for myself,
I would surely bring worldly troubles.
I earnestly withdrew from the world,
causing you all to suffer hunger and cold from a young age.
I was once moved by the words of Rúzhòng's virtuous wife,
wrapping myself in tattered cotton,
why feel ashamed before my sons?
This is one matter.
But I regret having no neighbors like Èr Zhòng,
no wife like Lái Fù at home,
holding this bitter heart,
truly feel inward shame.
In youth, I studied lute and books,
by chance loved tranquility,
opening a scroll and gaining insight,
I would joyfully forget to eat.
Seeing trees interweave their shade,
and seasonal birds change their songs,
again I felt happy and pleased.
I often said:
In the fifth or sixth month,
lying by the north window,
when a cool breeze briefly arrives,
I call myself a person from before Fú Xī's time.
With shallow thoughts and rare understanding,
I thought these words could last;
but as sun and moon passed by,
my knack for cleverness waned.
Longingly seeking the past,
how distant it seems.
Since falling ill,
I gradually approach decline and frailty.
Relatives and old friends do not forsake me,
often saving me with medicines and stones,
yet I fear my allotted lifespan will soon be limited.
You are all young and the family poor,
often burdened with the toil of fetching firewood and water,
when can this be avoided?
The thought stays in my heart,
how can it be expressed?
Yet although you are born of the same parent,
you should remember the principle that all within the four seas are brothers.
Bào Shū and Guǎn Zhòng,
divided wealth without suspicion;
Guī Shēng and Wǔ Jǔ,
spread thorns and recounted old times.
Thus, they could turn failure into success,
and achieve merit through loss.
If others can be like this,
how much more those of the same father?
Hán Yuáncháng of Yǐngchuān,
a renowned scholar of the late Hàn,
served as a high minister,
and died at seventy.
Brothers lived together,
until the end of their days.
Fàn Zhìchūn of Jìběi,
a man of integrity in the Jìn dynasty,
had seven generations sharing wealth,
with no resentful looks among family members.
The "Book of Songs" says:
'I look up to the high mountain,
I walk the great path.'
Though we cannot be like that,
sincerely revere it.
Be cautious!
What more have I to say.
"Elegy for My Younger Sister of the Chéng Family"
In the third year of the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
on the jiǎchén day of the fifth month,
the mourning period for my sister of the Chéng family has completed its second cycle.
I, Yuānmíng, offer a sacrifice of a shǎoláo,
bowing down to pour the libation.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Cold has passed and heat has come,
the sun and moon grow distant.
Dust accumulates on the beams,
the courtyard grass runs wild.
Lonely and empty the room,
plaintive are the orphaned children.
Food and wine offered in vain,
the departed, where have they gone!
Who is without brothers,
people share the same life,
but sigh for you and me,
bound by exceptional affection.
Our kind mother passed early,
we were still infant children.
I was but twelve years old,
you only nine.
Since our unknowing youth,
we grew up hand in hand.
Admirable, my virtuous sister,
endowed with virtue and integrity.
Quiet and respectful, seldom speaking,
hearing of goodness, she rejoiced.
Able to correct and harmonize,
both friendly and filial.
Her conduct within the women's quarters,
was a model to emulate.
I have heard that doing good,
brings blessings through one's own actions.
Why is Heaven so partial,
not granting this reward!
In the past, while in Jiānglíng,
we suffered Heaven's punishment again.
Brothers living apart,
separated like Chǔ and Yuè.
For you and me,
a hundred sorrows pierced our hearts.
Gloomy were the high clouds,
desolate the winter moon.
White snow veiled the dawn,
the long wind mourned the season.
Feeling overwhelmed, I wail aloud,
speaking of it, my tears turn to blood.
Reflecting on the past,
events feel not far away.
Letters still remain,
orphaned children fill my sight.
How could it be that once gone,
you never return for all eternity!
Silent and still the lofty hall,
when will you tread it again?

"Eulogy for My Cousin Jìngyuǎn"
In the year of xīnhài,
in the mid-autumn month,
on the nineteenth day,
my cousin Jìngyuǎn,
has chosen the hour for burial,
to rest eternally in the earth.
Moved by our lifelong companionship,
I grieve that once gone, he does not return.
My heart is pained and shattered,
tears well up and fill my eyes.
Thus, with garden fruits and seasonal wine,
I bid him farewell on his journey.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Oh, my brilliant brother,
endowed with integrity and spirit.
Filial since early youth,
friendly by nature's love.
With few desires and little scheming,
neither stubborn nor aloof.
Putting others before himself,
facing wealth, he thought of generosity.
His heart unattached to gain or loss,
his feelings unswayed by the world.
His countenance could be warm,
his words could be stern.
Delighting in noble friends,
he loved literature and arts.
The distant imperial realm,
stirred his wondrous heart,
abstaining from grains, abandoning duties,
he dwelt in seclusion by the southern mountains.
Gurgling were the hanging streams,
dim and shady the wild woods.
Gathering rare herbs at dawn,
playing the plain lute at dusk.
It is said the benevolent live long,
I secretly believed it alone.
How can these words,
only deceive me so!
Just past thirty years of age,
suddenly he left this world.
Long has he returned to the grave,
far and without return.
For you and me,
not merely close kin.
Our fathers were brothers,
our mothers were sisters.
Reaching the age of losing baby teeth,
we both suffered the loss of parents.
This bond was truly deep,
this affection truly strong.
Recalling those past days,
the joy of sharing a room.
In winter, lacking coarse garments,
in summer, thirsty with simple fare.
Supporting each other with principle,
cheering each other with smiles.
Was it not often lacking?
Yet we forgot hunger and cold.
I once tried an official career,
entangled in human affairs.
Wandering without achievement,
I feared betraying my pure aspirations.
Gathering my plans, I returned home,
you understood my intent.
I always wished to join hands,
setting aside others' opinions.
Often I recall autumn days,
when I went to harvest,
walking together with you,
sharing a boat to cross.
Staying three nights by the waterside,
joyfully drinking by the river.
The clear moon shone high,
the warm wind began to fade.
Holding cups, we spoke,
how things endure, but humans are fragile.
How is it, my brother,
you left this world before me!
Events cannot be retrieved,
thoughts, how can they end?
Days pass, months flow,
cold and heat alternate in rest.
Death and life are different realms,
existence and oblivion have their domains.
Awaiting the dawn of eternal return,
pointing the path, I ascend.
The babbling orphaned child,
cannot yet speak properly.
The sorrowful widow,
well-versed in rites and decorum.
The courtyard trees remain as before,
the study hall, empty and vast.
Who would say, Jìngyuǎn,
when will you return again?
I, merely a man,
am ignorant of such recent feelings.
The divination showed auspicious signs,
guiding our farewell journey.
Watching the banner fluttering afar,
holding the brush, my tears overflow.
If the spirits have awareness,
may they illuminate my sincere heart.
Alas, how sorrowful!
"Eulogy for Myself"
The year being Dīngmǎo,
the pitch standard corresponds to Wúyì.
The sky is cold, the nights long,
the winds bleak and desolate.
Wild geese are migrating,
plants and trees yellowing and falling.
I, Táozi, am about to leave the inn of this world,
returning forever to my original home.
Old friends grieve in sorrow,
gathering tonight for the farewell ceremony.
They offer fine vegetables as tribute,
present clear wine as libation.
My face has faded into darkness,
my voice grows ever more distant.
Alas, how mournful!
Vast is the great earth,
endless the high heavens.
They give birth to all things,
and I obtained human form.
Since becoming human,
I've encountered a fate of poverty.
My simple bowl and gourd often empty,
wearing summer cloth in winter.
I joyfully fetched water from the valley,
singing as I carried firewood.
Behind my shadowy brushwood gate,
I passed my days and nights.
As spring and autumn alternated,
I worked in the central garden.
Plowing and weeding,
nurturing and multiplying.
Delighting in plain texts,
harmonizing with the seven-string zither.
Basking in winter sun,
bathing in summer springs.
Though diligent without spare effort,
my mind remained constantly at ease.
Content with heaven and accepting my lot,
I hoped to reach a hundred years.
This span of a hundred years,
people cherish it.
Fearing they'll achieve nothing,
they treasure every day and moment.
Wishing to be valued while alive,
and remembered after death.
Alas, I alone marched differently,
always diverging from this.
Favor brought me no glory,
how could darkness stain me?
Alone in my humble hut,
drinking deeply and composing poetry.
Understanding fate and knowing destiny,
who could be without attachment?
Now that I transform,
I can depart without regret.
Having approached a century in age,
I admired reclusive retirement.
Following old age to its end,
what more is there to crave?
Cold and heat have passed by,
death differs from life.
good friends rush by night.
Bury me in the wilds,
to settle my soul.
Silent is my journey,
lonely the tomb gate.
Extravagant like the Sòng minister I'd mock,
frugal like the Wángsūn I'd laugh at.
Vast and already vanished,
sighing, now far away.
No mound, no marker tree,
as sun and moon pass on.
Not valuing former praise,
who cares for songs thereafter?
Life is truly hard,
what of death then?
Alas, how mournful!

"The Eight Schools of Confucianism"
After the Master passed away,
they scattered across the land,
established throughout the Central States,
forming the origins of the hundred schools,
becoming the Confucians of order and discipline.
Living in humble dwellings,
with wicker gates and small openings,
jar windows and rope-hinged doors,
eating one meal in two days,
dwelling in the Way—
these are the Confucians of the Way,
as practiced by the Zǐsī school.
Dressed in proper attire,
movements in compliance,
yielding greatly as if indifferent,
yielding slightly as if insincere—
this is the practice of the Zǐzhāng school.
The Yán school transmitted the Odes as their Way,
becoming the Confucians of remonstrance.
The Mèng school transmitted the Documents as their Way,
becoming the Confucians who clarify and reach far.
The Qīdiāo school transmitted the Rites as their Way,
becoming the Confucians of reverence, frugality, dignity, and respect.
The Zhòngliáng school transmitted Music as their Way,
harmonizing yin and yang,
becoming the Confucians who transform customs.
The Yuèzhèng school transmitted the Spring and Autumn Annals as their Way,
becoming the Confucians of rhetoric and historical analogy.
The Gōngsūn school transmitted the Changes as their Way,
becoming the Confucians of purity and subtlety.
"The Three Branches of Mohism"
Unfettered by customs,
unadorned by material things,
not esteeming fame,
not envious of the masses—
this is the Mohism of Sòng Xīng and Yǐn Wén.
Clad in coarse garments,
wearing straw sandals,
laboring day and night without rest,
taking self-suffering to the extreme—
this is the Mohism of Xiànglǐ Qín and Wǔ Hóuzǐ.
Both revered the classics but diverged in interpretation,
calling each other heterodox Mohists over the debate on hardness and whiteness—
this is the Mohism of Kǔ Huò, Sì Chǐ, and Dènglíngzǐ.

"Eulogy for Shàng Cháng and Qín Qìng"
Master Shàng once held a minor post,
with wife and children through morning and night.
In poverty or in wealth,
he read the Changes and understood gain and loss.
Master Qín excelled in wandering far,
his travels taking him ever distant.
He departed to seek famed mountains,
ascending peaks, unaware of return.
